sens: guardian of a prison, one who is responsible for the custody of prisoners
one who holds the key and authority in the place of detention
G1200.detail:
1. The jailer is literally one who watches over and guards prisoners in a prison. He is a man who has the responsibility to keep them safe. In the story of Paul and Silas in Philippi (Acts 16:23), the jailer is ordered to "keep them securely" after they have been thrown into prison for disturbing the peace.
2. The jailer is also one who holds power and access: he has the keys, he opens and closes the prison doors. When an earthquake shakes the prison and opens the doors (Acts 16:27), the jailer first believes that his prisoners have escaped and wants to commit suicide, knowing that he will be held responsible for their escape. Later (Acts 16:36), it is he who communicates to the prisoners the order of release from the authorities.
G1200.origine: The Greek word δεσμοφύλαξ is formed from two elements: δεσμός (desmos), which means "bond" or "chain," and φύλαξ (phylax), which means "guardian" or "watchman." It is therefore literally a "guardian of the chains" or "guardian of the bonds." In Acts 16, the word ἀρχιδεσμοφύλαξ (archi-desmophulax) is also found, meaning the "chief jailer," indicating that there could be a hierarchy among prison guards. This descriptive terminology is typical of Greek, which constructs words by combining roots to express a function or role.
G1200.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the account of Acts 16, during the imprisonment of Paul and Silas in Philippi. In this context, the jailer plays a central role in the conversion of the heart: first an adversary of the apostles (he keeps them "securely"), he becomes a believer after the miracle of the earthquake and the subsequent conversion. This story shows how an encounter with the power of God transforms even one who seems to be on the side of the persecutors. The term is used without variation in meaning: it always refers to the man responsible for executing the orders of civil authorities inside the prison.
G1200.portee: This story of the jailer in Philippi is a powerful illustration of grace: the one who was paid to imprison believers becomes a believer himself and hastens to tend to the wounds of Paul and Silas (verses 33-34). This shows that no one is too far from faith, not even one who serves an unjust system. The jailer asks, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" — a question that reveals how the Gospel can break down the thickest walls, including those of a prison.

sens: Building or enclosed place where prisoners are held
Captivity, imprisonment
G1201.detail:
1. A prison is a closed, guarded building designed to hold prisoners. In Acts 5:21-23, the apostles are sought at the prison, which turns out to be securely locked with guards at the gates — this place of detention is therefore a robust construction, with security measures.
2. The word also refers to the state of captivity itself, the imprisonment to which one is subjected. When Matthew 11:2 says that John heard about the works of Christ in "his prison," it refers to the place where John the Baptist was held captive by order of Herod.
G1201.origine: The Greek word δεσμωτήριον comes from δεσμός (desmos), which means "bond" or "chain." It is therefore literally "the place of bonds," the house where prisoners are chained. The root evokes the image of chains and fetters. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word translates the Hebrew בֵּית סֹהַר (beth sohar), "house of guard," which appears in the account of Joseph imprisoned in Egypt.
G1201.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels and Acts. Matthew 11:2 uses it to refer to the dungeon of John the Baptist in Judea. The three occurrences in Acts (5:21, 23, and 16:26) describe situations of persecution: the apostles are imprisoned by the religious authorities, and later Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi. In these three cases from Acts, the context emphasizes the closed and secure nature of the place: the doors are locked, the guards are on duty, until divine intervention (angels or earthquake) breaks these bonds.
G1201.portee: The prison is an instrument of persecution against the witnesses of Christ. These accounts show that physical captivity cannot silence either the word of John the Baptist or that of the apostles: what was meant to confine faith actually exposes it to the light. For the Christian reader, these passages remind us that following Jesus may cost freedom, but that this captivity is never the final word of God.

sens: Person detained in captivity, chained or confined for committing a crime or offense
Person held against their will by a public or military authority
G1202.detail:
1. A prisoner is someone who has lost their freedom and is held in captivity. In Acts 27:1, Paul is delivered as a "prisoner" to a centurion: he is chained and placed under military guard to be taken to Rome for his trial. This is the legal captivity of a person being judged or awaiting judgment.
2. The word also broadly refers to any person held captive, particularly in a military or wartime context. In Acts 27:42, the soldiers want to kill the "prisoners" to prevent them from escaping by swimming: these are captives whose escape is feared.
G1202.origine: The Greek word δεσμώτης (desmōtēs) comes from δεσμός (desmos), which means "chain" or "bond." A prisoner is literally someone who is "bound," attached by chains. The Hebrew word אסר (asar) in the Old Testament, translated by this term in Greek, also carries the idea of binding and captivity.
G1202.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in Acts 27 during Paul's journey to Rome. In Acts 27:1, it is used in the singular for Paul himself, showing his legal status as a political captive sent for trial. In Acts 27:42, it is in the plural to refer to prisoners of war or common law prisoners aboard the ship. In both cases, the context is that of legal captivity under Roman authority during a sea voyage.
G1202.portee: This word reminds us that Paul's captivity, though painful, was not a defeat of his testimony. In this same chapter, it is Paul who saves the centurion and the entire crew from shipwreck by proclaiming the word of God. Being a prisoner from the world's perspective does not prevent one from being free in Christ and bearing His message.

sens: One who owns a slave or servant and exercises absolute authority over them
An owner, a boss in a relationship of power and dependence
God or Christ recognized as sovereign Lord
G1203.detail:
1. The master is primarily the owner of slaves or servants who are entirely submissive to him and must serve him with respect. In 1 Timothy 6:1, Paul exhorts slaves to honor their masters, which shows that this relationship of dependence was a reality of ancient life.
2. More broadly, a master is one who holds authority, complete control over someone or something — a boss, an owner. In 2 Timothy 2:21, Paul speaks of being "a vessel for honor, useful to his master," using the word to designate the one to whom the vessel belongs.
3. The word designates God or Christ as sovereign Lord, the one on whom we are absolutely dependent. In Acts 4:24, the disciples cry out, "Lord, you who made heaven and earth," recognizing God as the ultimate master. This meaning emphasizes unquestioned authority and total power.
G1203.origine: The word comes from a Greek root expressing domination and absolute control. It is much stronger than "lord" in the common sense: where the Greek κύριος (kyrios) designates a superior or a responsible person, δεσπότης emphasizes exclusive possession and unlimited power — like a master over his slave. In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew word אָדוֹן (adon), the lord or master.
G1203.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles and the general epistles. In 1 Timothy, Titus, and 2 Timothy, it refers to slave masters that Christian servants must honor, showing how the early Church addressed a slaveholding society. But δεσπότης rises well above this earthly reality: it is used as a title for God (Luke 2:29, Acts 4:24, Revelation 6:10) and applied to Christ (2 Peter 2:1, Jude 1:4), affirming that only the Lord holds absolute authority and ownership.
G1203.portee: This word reminds the reader that all human power is only temporary and relative. Earthly masters themselves are merely servants of a greater Master. For the believer, recognizing God or Christ as "despotès" means accepting to be entirely at His service, not with a servile fear, but with the joy of one who knows they are loved by their Lord. This liberates from the fear of the powerful of this world.

sens: To come towards someone, to head towards a place
To approach, to arrive near
To come in response to a call
To approach a source or origin
To be present, to exist up to a given moment
G1204.detail:
1. The word δεῦρο expresses movement towards the speaker or towards a specific place. It is a direct call: "Come here!" When Jesus says to the rich young man, "Then come, and follow me" (Matthew 19:21), he calls him to draw closer and follow him. It is a concrete movement, an invitation to change places.

2. The word can also simply mean to present oneself or to arrive. When Jesus shouts, "Lazarus, come out!" (John 11:43), he commands Lazarus to leave the tomb and come to him. The idea is to come out from a place and show oneself.

3. In Acts 7:3 and 7:34, God says to Abraham and then to Moses: "Go" — these are divine orders to accomplish a mission, to move forward. The emphasis is less on approaching than on obedience to the commanded movement.

4. The word can evoke the idea of a presence that comes to us, especially in Revelation: "Come and see" (Revelation 17:1, 21:9) invites to approach and contemplate.
G1204.origine: The word δεῦρο is an adverb of ancient Greek origin that literally means "this way, here." It comes from a root expressing direction and proximity. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew לֵךְ or לֵכָה, which are the imperative forms of the verb "to go": direct orders, immediate calls. It is a particularly vivid word, marked by the urgency and authority of the one who speaks.
G1204.emploi: The word δεῦρο appears 9 times in the New Testament. Jesus uses it to call his disciples or crowds to follow him or to come closer: "Come, follow me" (Matthew 19:21, Mark 10:21, Luke 18:22). It is a personal, direct call, often in a context of conversion or commitment. In John 11:43, it is a miraculous command addressed to Lazarus. In Acts, God uses it to send Abraham and Moses on a mission (Acts 7:3, 7:34): it is then a divine order to accomplish a work. In Revelation (17:1, 21:9), it is an invitation to contemplate heavenly visions. The word always carries the idea of an immediate break with what was, to turn towards what is requested.
G1204.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that Jesus addresses direct and personal calls. Like the rich young man, everyone receives the invitation "Come, follow me" — it is a word that sets in motion, that demands a decision. The word also expresses that God acts with authority and urgency: He does not ask for permission; He commands because He sees what is necessary. It is a transformative call.

sens: Call to draw near, to come to a place
Invitation to join an action or to follow someone
Order or exhortation directed at several people
Urgent call to participate or to appropriate something
G1205.detail:
1. The word simply invites to move, to come towards the one who speaks. It is a direct call: "Come see a man who told me all that I ever did" (John 4:29), the Samaritan woman calls her neighbors to come meet Jesus.
2. It can also exhort to follow someone or to act together. "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:19): Jesus uses this word to invite the disciples to follow him, to join his mission.
3. Often it is an order addressed to several, a command that imposes itself. "Come, you who are blessed by my Father; inherit the kingdom" (Matthew 25:34): the king invites the elect to take possession of their reward.
4. The word also carries the urgency of a decisive action. In the parable of the tenants (Matthew 21:38), "Come, let us kill him" expresses a sudden and pressing common will.
G1205.origine: This word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "go" or "come"; it is a direct call to motion, to move towards someone. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it often translates the Hebrew "lekhu," which carries the same meaning: an order or an invitation to get moving. The word belongs to the family of verbs of movement and direct action.
G1205.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, John) and Revelation. Jesus uses it to call his disciples (Matthew 4:19, Mark 1:17) or to invite the crowds to come to him (Matthew 11:28). It is also used for public exhortation: the angel says to the women, "Come" near the tomb (Matthew 28:6), Jesus invites the guests to the wedding (Matthew 22:4). In the parables, it is a call to common action or judgment (Matthew 25:34, Revelation 19:17). The word always retains its urgency and personal call.
G1205.portee: This word reveals how God and Christ call: not by cold constraint, but by a direct, warm invitation that involves freedom and closeness. Hearing "Come" from the mouth of Jesus or the Father is to be personally solicited, invited to communion and action. For the believer, it is also a reminder that responding to this call means giving oneself to the Lord and His mission.

sens: The day that immediately follows
Figuratively: what comes after, in a succession
G1206.detail:
1. The next day: it is the day that comes after today. In Acts 28:13, Paul and his companions sail from Syracuse to Reggio, and then "the next day" a south wind rises, allowing them to reach Puteoli in two days. The word simply refers to this second day of travel.
2. More broadly, the word can qualify anything that happens second, after a first occurrence, in a series of events or moments.
G1206.origine: The word comes from "second" (δεύτερος). It is an adjective that has retained an adverbial nuance: it does not only say "which is second," but "during the second day," "at the time of the second day." That is why it is often used without an article, as a sort of time complement.
G1206.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:13. It is found in the account of Paul's journey to Rome, at the moment when the boat progresses from Syracuse to Reggio and then to Puteoli. Paul and his companions travel in stages; "the next day" after leaving Syracuse, the wind changes and allows them to advance. The context is that of a natural succession of days during a maritime journey.
G1206.portee: This simple word reminds us that the Bible also notes the concrete details of journeys and historical events. It is not only concerned with spectacular miracles but also with ordinary conditions — the wind, the time it takes to travel. This emphasizes that the Gospel is rooted in real history, where God guides His people day by day.

sens: Enigmatic adjective designating a particular Sabbath, the exact meaning of which remains uncertain
G1207.detail: 1. The term "second-first" or "called second-first" appears only once in the Bible to qualify a Sabbath day (Luke 6:1). Scholars who have studied this passage are uncertain about its exact meaning: it could refer to a special Sabbath in the Jewish calendar, perhaps the second Sabbath after the first day of Passover, or a Sabbath with a cultic particularity. The text itself remains obscure, and several ancient manuscripts diverge on its wording.
G1207.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: "deutero" (second) and "prôtos" (first), awkwardly juxtaposed in Greek. This strange construction suggests that the term could be a transcription or an imprecise transliteration of an Aramaic or Hebrew expression from the Jewish calendar. The lack of a clear parallel in other Greek or Hebrew texts means there is no satisfactory explanation.
G1207.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:1, in the context of Jesus and His disciples passing through grain fields on a Sabbath and plucking heads of grain to eat. Ancient commentators have proposed various interpretations (a second Sabbath in the same week, a particular Sabbath of the priestly calendar), but none has gained unanimous acceptance. The existence of several manuscript variants suggests that the scribes themselves found this term difficult to convey with certainty.
G1207.portee: This word illustrates the limits of our understanding of the details of the calendar and Jewish practices of the time. It reminds us that the Gospel was written in a specific cultural context, with its usages and conventions that time has partially obscured. Rather than focusing on the precise identification of the Sabbath, the reader can concentrate on the essence of the narrative: Jesus, confronted with the rest of the Sabbath, shows that human need takes precedence over strict ritual observances.

sens: which comes after the first in an order or series
which occurs or returns a second time
which occupies a rank immediately below the first
in a list, the element number two
G1208.detail:
1. Second designates what comes in order after the first. Matthew 22:26 speaks of the "second" and "third" brother in the story of the resurrection, in order of succession in the sibling relationship.
2. Second can also mean a repetition, a second occurrence of the same action or event. Acts 10:15 reports that a voice was heard "for the second time," meaning it returned a second time. Hebrews 9:28 speaks of the "second" coming of Christ, which will follow the first historical coming.
3. In a ranking, second describes what is in the second position, immediately after the first. 1 Corinthians 12:28 lists: "God has appointed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers."
4. By extension, the word can qualify what is of second order, of second rank, less important or less excellent than the first. Hebrews 8:7 contrasts the "old covenant" with a "second" (better) covenant, suggesting a gradation of value.
G1208.origine: The Greek word deuteros comes from an Indo-European root meaning "two." It is related to δύο (two) and carries the fundamental idea of duality and ordinal rank. The suffix -ος makes it an ordinal adjective, transforming the cardinal "two" into the ordinal "second." In ancient Greek, this adjective consistently designates the position two in an order.
G1208.emploi: Deuteros is used approximately 44 times in the New Testament, widely in the Gospels and the epistles. It serves to indicate an order of succession (the second of the disciples, the second of the brothers), a temporal repetition (to come a second time, to write a second letter), or a ranking (second in importance or function). In Revelation, it is notably found in enumerations (the second seal, the second angel, the second plague). The figurative sense also appears: "the second death" (Revelation 2:11, 20:14, 21:8) refers to a form of spiritual death, distinct from physical death, marking a different order or category.
G1208.portee: This simple word reminds the believer that the Christian life and the history of salvation are marked by passages, stages, renewed beginnings. The "second time" of forgiveness, the "second coming" of Christ, the "second death" warn that not everything is fixed after a first occurrence. This invites vigilance: a second chance may follow a first, but so may a second consequence from first acts.

sens: To take, accept something that is offered or entrusted to you
To welcome someone kindly, to treat them as a guest
To mentally accept a word, a person, a doctrine
To take with oneself, to admit into one's home
G1209.detail:
1. To receive primarily means to take possession of something that is presented or offered to you. You receive a document, a garment, a chalice (Luke 22:17), or even an order as Paul receives letters from Damascus (Acts 22:5).
2. The word also applies to the kind welcome of a person: to receive someone means to treat them generously, to house them, to show them friendship. Jesus speaks of receiving children, taking them in his arms (Luke 2:28), and receiving a prophet or a righteous person (Matthew 10:40, 10:41).
3. Receiving takes on an inner and spiritual meaning when it comes to accepting a word, a doctrine, a teaching: to receive the word of God (Acts 8:14), to receive the Gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4), to receive the grace of God (2 Corinthians 6:1). It is to welcome into one's heart and thoughts.
4. Finally, to receive the kingdom of God (Mark 10:15) means to admit and welcome it as a present reality and transformative power, with the openness of a child.
G1209.origine: The verb δέχομαι comes from a root that evokes the idea of taking or seizing. The base word is simple and ancient in biblical Greek. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew לקח (to take). The verb is associated with many prefixes to nuance its meaning: to welcome (προσδέχομαι), to receive in return (ἀποδέχομαι), to receive from all sides (περιδέχομαι), etc.
G1209.emploi: The verb δέχομαι appears 46 times in the New Testament. It is very frequent in Luke (Gospel and Acts), who often describes how people welcome Jesus or his disciples. Mark and Matthew also use it, especially in Jesus' teaching about the kingdom. The word has two major uses: (1) the material and concrete action of taking or welcoming (letters, a child, a traveler), and (2) the spiritual and mental acceptance (to receive the Word, grace, the Gospel). In Acts, we see believers receive the word of God eagerly (17:11, 1:6). For Paul, to receive also means to accept a person or grace with all one's heart.
G1209.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is not primarily an effort or a conquest, but a welcome: we receive the kingdom, we receive grace, we receive the word as we receive a gift. It is an act of humility and trust, similar to the attitude of a child with Jesus. For the believer, receiving also engages generosity: to welcome a disciple of Christ or a stranger is to receive him (Matthew 10:40). This verb invites both receptive abandonment and welcoming generosity.

sens: To tie, fasten with a rope or chain
To wrap tightly (a body, limbs)
To restrain, imprison someone
To hold someone bound morally or physically (sickness, sin)
To obligate, submit to a law or rule
To prohibit, declare forbidden (religious language)
G1210.detail:
1. The primary meaning is material: to fix something with a rope or a tie. One binds a donkey to a door (Mark 11:4), or a large sheet by its four corners (Acts 10:11).

2. The word applies to the wrapping of a corpse: one wraps the body of Jesus in linen (John 19:40), or ties the feet of Lazarus with strips of cloth (John 11:44).

3. To bind takes on the meaning of "to capture and imprison": soldiers bind Jesus (John 18:12), Peter binds the prisoners he brings to Jerusalem (Acts 22:5), Paul speaks of those he bound in the synagogues (Acts 9:2).

4. The word also expresses an invisible domination: Satan binds a woman through illness (Luke 13:16), or the word of God is not bound despite Paul's imprisonment (2 Timothy 2:9).

5. To bind means "to submit to an obligation": a woman is bound to her husband by marriage (Romans 7:2; 1 Corinthians 7:39), a person can be bound by a constraint (Acts 20:22).

6. In Jewish religious language, to bind means "to prohibit, declare illicit": Jesus grants Peter the power to bind on earth (Matthew 16:19, 18:18), that is to decide what is forbidden.
G1210.origine: The verb δέω comes from a primitive root meaning "to tie, bind." In ancient Hebrew, this word often translates אסר (assar), which has the same concrete meaning: to bind with ropes or chains. The family of the Greek word includes δεσμή (the binding, the tie) and δεσμός (the chain, the prison). The word retains both dimensions: the physical act of tying and, by extension, constraint, obligation, or prohibition.
G1210.emploi: The verb δέω appears 41 times in the New Testament. It is used first for concrete actions: tying animals (Matthew 21:2; Mark 11:2), wrapping a corpse (John 19:40; John 11:44). The meaning of "to imprison or capture" is very frequent: prisoners, demoniacs, criminals are bound (Mark 5:3-4; Acts 9:2; Acts 22:5). Paul and John also use the word figuratively to describe invisible bonds: Satan binds through illness (Luke 13:16), marriage binds spouses (Romans 7:2), the word of God cannot be bound by any chain (2 Timothy 2:9). Finally, in Matthew and John, Jesus uses "to bind" in the sense of "to declare forbidden" when he grants Peter the power to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19; 18:18), a rabbinic language designating doctrinal authority.
G1210.portee: This word helps the believer grasp the physical and spiritual reality of imprisonment, captivity, and liberation. It shows that prayer and faith can unbind visible and invisible chains — Satan binds, but God and his Church can unbind (cf. "to bind and to loose"). It also reminds us that marriage is a solemn bond, and that the Word of God, even when its witnesses are chained, cannot be bound. For the reader, it is an invitation to seek deliverance from all that binds them through Christ.

sens: Particle that reinforces the affirmation or command
Marks a logical conclusion or consequence
Emphasizes the importance or urgency of what is said
Provides more precision and clarity to the statement
G1211.detail:
1. Δή is a small Greek particle that attaches to a word or phrase to highlight and strengthen it. It has no exact equivalent in English, but it functions like an accent that the speaker places on what they are saying: "Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:20) — the "therefore" here does not draw from a prior conclusion, it strongly affirms: we must glorify God now.

2. It also marks a transition or a new stage in the discourse: "Paul said to Barnabas: Let us return and visit the brothers" (Acts 15:36) — it emphasizes that the decided action naturally follows from the present situation.

3. With an imperative or command, it reinforces the command itself: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul" (Acts 13:2) — it is a weighty, supported command.

4. With a present statement, it gives more certainty and weight to what is affirmed: "Surely it is not angels that he helps" (Hebrews 2:16) — it is an assertion posed as definitive and clear.
G1211.origine: Δή is a primitive particle in Greek that has no clear etymology. It mainly appears in lively, oratory, or narrative styles, where it serves to give emphasis to speech. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to particles like הִנָּה ("behold") or אָז ("then"), which also mark insistence or transition. It is a tool of spoken Greek that found its place in the New Testament to animate discourse and make it more persuasive.
G1211.emploi: Δή appears six times in the passages provided by the Segond. It is mainly found in the words of Jesus and the apostles, and in apostolic instructions. With an imperative or command, it reinforces the command (Acts 13:2, 1 Corinthians 6:20). With a present affirmation or rhetorical question, it gives more emphasis and certainty (Hebrews 2:16). It can also mark a transition or practical conclusion in a discourse (Acts 15:36). The Segond translates it variously according to the context: "therefore," "part," "indeed" — which shows that it does not have a fixed equivalent but always plays a role of emphasis.
G1211.portee: This small particle teaches the reader that every word of God is weighed and presented with strength. When the Word says "Therefore glorify God," this "therefore" is not a detail: it marks the urgency and seriousness of the call. It invites us to listen attentively and to recognize that Scripture does not speak in vain, but with intention and authority. This strengthens confidence in the inspired Word.

sens: visible, clear to perception
clear to the mind, understood unequivocally
revealed by signs or indications
G1212.detail:
1. Evident in the primary sense: what stands out, what can be seen clearly. When Peter's language "makes him recognized" as a disciple of Jesus (Matthew 26:73), it is because his Galilean accent betrays him visibly: it is a manifest and undeniable sign.
2. Evident in the sense of "known to the mind": what is understood unambiguously, what one is certain of. When Paul asserts "it is evident that he who subjected all things to him is excepted" (1 Corinthians 15:27), he means that it is a logical conclusion, impossible to contest.
3. Evident as a result of deduction: what becomes clear once one reflects. "It is evident that we can take nothing with us" (1 Timothy 6:7): the truth imposes itself on common sense.
G1212.origine: Greek δῆλος: an adjective meaning primarily "visible, apparent." The root suggests the idea of what shows itself, what cannot be hidden. Different from φανερός ("manifest, shown"), δῆλος emphasizes more what is clear to the mind, understood and recognized by the observer.
G1212.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in the neuter substantive form "δῆλον ἐστιν" ("it is evident") or as an attribute. It serves to introduce a truth that the author affirms as undeniable: a visibility (Matthew 26:73), a logical deduction (1 Corinthians 15:27, Galatians 3:11), a moral evidence (1 Timothy 6:7). In each case, it is a certainty that is stated, not a supposition.
G1212.portee: This word teaches us to recognize that certain spiritual truths do not require complicated proofs: they are evident to the good sense of the Christian. The death of Christ for us, the impossibility of accumulating eternal riches, justification by faith — all this becomes evident when we receive the word of God with a sincere heart.

sens: Communicate information to someone
Reveal or show something clearly
Render evident, manifest
G1213.detail:
1. The simplest sense is to transmit information, to make something known to someone. It is to inform someone of what they did not know. For example, Paul writes to the Corinthians: "I have been informed concerning you, by those of Chloe, that there are divisions among you" (1 Corinthians 1:11) — someone communicated news to him.
2. The word also designates the action of revealing or bringing to light what was hidden. On the day of judgment, "the fire will test what sort of work each one has done" (1 Corinthians 3:13) — the fire will make known, will render visible the true nature of the works. It is to show clearly what was concealed.
3. Finally, the word means to mark, indicate, point out something. When Scripture says "once more," these words "indicate the removal of those things that are shaken" (Hebrews 12:27) — they signal, they manifest this change to our minds.
G1213.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to make manifest, to show." It is formed on the base δῆλος (dèlos), "visible, clear, manifest." Greek uses this word mainly to "make known" something to the mind or understanding — rather than simply making it visible to the eyes (this is the nuance with other similar verbs). In Greek of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "ydaʿ," which means "to know" or "to make known."
G1213.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the apostolic epistles. In Paul, it serves to describe how information is communicated or verified: "I have learned" (1 Corinthians 1:11), or how works will be revealed at judgment (1 Corinthians 3:13). In the author of the epistle to the Hebrews, it means "to indicate" or "to signify" in a more formal sense (Hebrews 12:27). In the epistles of Peter and in Paul's letter to the Colossians, the word describes knowledge that comes from God or his messengers: "has made known to us what kind of love the Spirit has for you" (Colossians 1:8), "the glory that would follow" (1 Peter 1:11).
G1213.portee: This verb reminds us that knowledge of God and his will comes to us through revelation and communication — not through our own insight. It also emphasizes that our Christian work will one day be manifested and tested: nothing will remain hidden from God's sight. It is an invitation to live in awareness of this future clarity.

sens: Companion of the apostle Paul
The one who abandoned Paul for the love of the present world
G1214.detail:
1. Demas is a man who accompanied the apostle Paul during part of his ministry. He is mentioned alongside other faithful collaborators like Luke the physician and Mark (Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 1:24).

2. However, at the end of Paul's life, Demas abandoned him, motivated by his attachment to the things of the present world. Paul reports this with a certain sadness in writing to Timothy that Demas "has forsaken me, having loved this present world, and has departed for Thessalonica" (2 Timothy 4:10). His story illustrates how even a companion in ministry can turn away from the faith due to love for the world.
G1214.origine: The name Demas is probably a shortened form of the Greek name Demetrius (which means "dedicated to Demeter," the goddess of the harvest). It is a common name in the Greco-Roman world. Its occurrence in the New Testament is limited to the three passages mentioned, making him a figure known primarily through his association with Paul and his subsequent abandonment.
G1214.emploi: Demas appears three times in the New Testament, always in connection with Paul. First, he is presented as a fellow worker of Paul, alongside prominent figures like Luke, Mark, and Aristarchus. Later, in Paul's last letter before his martyrdom (2 Timothy), the apostle mentions his painful departure, marking a striking contrast: from a faithful helper in ministry, Demas becomes an example of one who turns away from the Gospel for the pleasures of the world. His personal story illustrates the tensions between devotion to Christ and the allure of temporal realities.
G1214.portee: The story of Demas warns the reader that proximity to Christian ministry is not a guarantee of perseverance in faith. It shows that it is possible to begin serving the Lord faithfully but to be seduced by "the love of this present world" — comfort, security, or simple earthly pleasures. His abandonment of Paul invites every believer to examine their own priorities and to guard their heart against the gradual weakening of their commitment to Christ.

sens: To speak in front of an assembly with authority
To deliver an official speech to the people
G1215.detail:
1. To address publicly means to speak in front of a crowd or assembly, particularly to express something important or official. The word evokes the image of a speaker who stands up and speaks with authority to their audience. In Acts 12:21, Herod, dressed in royal robes and sitting on his throne, addresses the people publicly — he solemnly speaks to the assembled crowd before him.
2. This term emphasizes the public and official nature of the speech, not a private conversation but a discourse intended for a group. The speaker seeks to communicate something serious or important to all at once, like a king announcing a decision or making himself heard by the people.
G1215.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: *dêmos* (the people, the assembly) and *agoreúō* (to speak to the assembly, hence "agora," the public square). The initial image is that of a citizen standing up at the agora — the heart of public life — to speak to the gathered people. It is a word specifically formed to designate this kind of official and solemn speech.
G1215.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:21, where King Herod addresses the assembled people publicly. The context is that of a solemn scene: Herod is dressed in his royal robes, sitting on his throne, and addressing the crowd. It is an official moment of power and public communication. The word underscores that this is not an ordinary speech but a royal address, delivered before witnesses.
G1215.portee: This passage reminds us that all human power, even when clothed in royal splendor, is subject to God. Herod speaks these words full of pride, but God judges him immediately. For the Christian reader, this word emphasizes the importance of public speech and calls for great sobriety: the one who speaks to the people bears a great responsibility before God.

sens: Silversmith from Ephesus who made silver shrines for the goddess Diana
Christian disciple praised for his faithfulness to the faith
G1216.detail:
1. Demetrius is a craftsman from Ephesus (Acts 19:24) who makes miniature temples in silver dedicated to the goddess Diana. He employs several workers and makes a lot of money from this trade. When the apostle Paul preaches the Gospel in Ephesus, people abandon idolatry, which threatens Demetrius's sales and income. He then decides to oppose Paul by inciting a riot (Acts 19:38).
2. Another Demetrius, a Christian disciple, is mentioned in the letter of 3 John. The apostle John warmly commends him: all who know him, "and the truth itself," testify to his uprightness and faithfulness to the Gospel (3 John 1:12). Unlike the first, this Demetrius is a model of authentic faith.
G1216.origine: The Greek name Δημήτριος comes from Δημήτηρ (Demeter), the Greek goddess of agriculture and harvest. It literally means "dedicated to Demeter" or "belonging to Demeter." It was a common name in the Greco-Roman world, borne by several people of various ranks and functions.
G1216.emploi: There are only three occurrences of the name Demetrius in the New Testament referring to two distinct individuals. The first is Demetrius the silversmith (Acts 19:24, 38), a businessman operating in Ephesus during Paul's mission. His commercial interests come into direct conflict with the preaching of the Gospel. The second is a Christian (3 John 1:12) whom John highly recommends to his correspondent, thus highlighting the moral and religious contrasts that the same name can represent in apostolic history.
G1216.portee: These two Demetrius embody two opposing paths: one who clings to money and idolatry in the face of the Gospel, and the one who embraces faith with integrity. For the Christian reader, this contrast serves as a reminder that true treasure is not material wealth, but faithfulness to the truth of Christ and a reputation based on spiritual authenticity.

sens: one who designs and constructs a building or a city
one who creates or manufactures something
God as the creator of the world
G1217.detail:
1. In its primary sense, the word refers to a builder, someone who imagines and realizes a structure: this is why it is translated as "architect." In Hebrews 11:10, Abraham awaits "the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God" — the image is that of a magnificently built city, which God himself has conceived and constructed.
2. More broadly, the word applies to any creator or manufacturer: one who designs and realizes a work, whether material or spiritual. The meaning then shifts from "builder" to "author." 
3. In particular, Greek philosophical tradition used it to designate God as the Creator of the world — not in the sense of one who created it from nothing, but as one who gave form to what exists, like an architect who organizes and structures his material.
G1217.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: "demos" (the people) and "ergon" (the work, the labor). Originally, it designated one who works for the people, or who accomplishes a work of public interest. Gradually, the meaning expanded to encompass any builder and creator. The word "creator" (ktistès) and the word "artisan" (technitès) are its close relatives; the Greek Bible often translates Hebrew words referring to divine creation with this term.
G1217.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:10. It is used to describe God as the one who founded and built the heavenly city — this "city whose architect is God." It is a rare word that emphasizes God's creative wisdom: not only has He conceived this city, but He has also solidly built it on unshakeable foundations. The context is that of Abraham's faith, who hopes for a permanent dwelling beyond this world.
G1217.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is not a distant and indifferent creator, but one who designs with wisdom and realizes with authority. Like an architect who draws the plans for his work, God has planned and constructed the world, and especially the eternal city where His children will dwell. For the believer, this invites trust: there exists a "city that has foundations," not built by man, but by God Himself.

sens: A region, a territory
The entire population of a city or state
Citizens gathered in a public assembly
The common people, as opposed to magistrates and the powerful
G1218.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a district or country — a geographical and administrative area. This is the most concrete sense of the term.

2. It then extends to encompass all the inhabitants of a region or city, taken as a political community. It is "the people" in the sense of the political body of a city like Ephesus or Thessalonica.

3. Very often in Acts, the word specifically designates the gathered citizens — the popular assembly that comes together at the sound of the trumpet or tambourine. When Paul "wanted to present himself before the people" (Acts 19:30), it refers to the crowd assembled to deliberate.

4. The word also carries a nuance of class: it is the populace, the mass of ordinary people — in contrast to magistrates, leaders, and scholars. In Acts 17:5, the "populace" is the dregs of society, those "wicked men" whom the jealous Jews recruit to cause trouble.
G1218.origine: The Greek word δῆμος comes from a root meaning "to divide" or "to distribute" — hence the idea of a region or section of territory. In ancient Greece, a demos was a neighborhood in Athens or an administrative subdivision. It is related to words like "democrat" (the power of the people). In the Septuagint, it often translates the Hebrew משׁפחה (mishpakhah), meaning family or clan, broadening the sense to organized community.
G1218.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in Acts and always in the plural or in the context of a public assembly. Each time it designates the common people as a political body — either gathered or in motion. In Acts 12:22, it is the crowd that applauds the king. In Acts 17:5 and 19:30-33, it is the assembled people that Paul's enemies seek to mobilize against him. The word emphasizes less compassion for the people than its role as a political force, capable of creating disturbances or being manipulated by agitators.
G1218.portee: This word reminds the reader of the weight of the people as a political actor — their ability to gather, to be influenced, to act en masse. In Acts, it shows how the crowd can become a formidable weapon in the hands of the enemies of the Gospel. It is a reminder that apostolic preaching must confront not only the leaders but also popular movements, sometimes manipulated by jealousy or deceit.

sens: belonging to the people, to the community
taking place in front of everyone, visible to all
openly, without secrecy
G1219.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what belongs to the community, to the people as a whole. In Acts 5:18, the apostles are thrown "into the public prison," meaning the city prison, that of the civic community, not a private prison.
2. From this derives the meaning of "before all" or "in the presence of all." In Acts 16:37, Paul protests: they were beaten "publicly," meaning that everyone saw this punishment, which makes the affront even more serious.
3. By extension, the word also means "openly, without reservation." In Acts 20:20, Paul asserts: "I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house" — he speaks both in front of assemblies and with an open heart, without hiding anything of his message.
G1219.origine: The word comes from δῆμος (dèmos), which means "people" in the sense of civic community, and the suffix -ος which forms adjectives. It is the same Greek as the French word "démocratie." In the New Testament, δημόσιος retains this link to the people and communal life: what is public is what concerns the majority, what is of public knowledge.
G1219.emploi: The word appears four times in Acts, particularly during Paul's ministry in Jerusalem and Asia. It first qualifies the prison itself (Acts 5:18), then the adverb "publicly" describes the manner of acting or speaking: being beaten publicly (16:37), preaching publicly (18:28, 20:20). In these passages, Paul, by his insistence on the public nature of his actions and what has happened to him, claims that everything should be done in the light of day, without secrecy. It is an affirmation of dignity and transparency.
G1219.portee: This word reminds the Christian that faith is not a hidden or shameful matter: it is confessed before all. Paul, like the apostles, is not afraid to testify openly, even if it costs him. It is a call to frankness and courage in the life of faith, to not be ashamed of the Gospel, but to proclaim it without reservation or excessive caution.

sens: Roman currency of average value, used in everyday transactions
Daily wage of a laborer
Unit price or market value of something
G1220.detail:
1. The denarius is a Roman silver coin, the standard currency of the Roman Empire during the New Testament times. It is the Greek equivalent of the drachma. Denarii can be seen circulating in markets and ordinary transactions: one hundred denarii represents an amount that a servant owes another (Matthew 18:28), or two hundred denarii is the price for a large quantity of bread (Mark 6:37).

2. The denarius is also the standard daily wage of a laborer. In the parable of the workers in the vineyard, Jesus states that a denarius is the agreed price for a day's work: the workers hired in the morning receive a denarius for their day (Matthew 20:2, 13), just like those hired later (Matthew 20:9).

3. The denarius is used to express the price or value of something precious: pure nard poured on Jesus could have been sold for three hundred denarii (Mark 14:5), and John specifies that this could have fed the poor. It is a measure of wealth and exchange.
G1220.origine: The word δηνάριον comes from the Latin denarius, the official Roman coin. Greek borrowed it as is, as it was the political and economic reality: the Greek provinces of the Roman Empire used the Roman denarius. The Latin word denarius itself comes from "deni," meaning ten, as at that time it was worth about ten times the as (small bronze coin). It is a borrowing that attests to Roman dominance in the biblical world of the first century.
G1220.emploi: The word δηνάριον appears 15 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the first three Gospels and Revelation. It is a concrete currency, never abstract. Matthew uses it 8 times, especially in economic parables (the unforgiving debtor, the workers in the vineyard, the tax to Caesar). Mark mentions it 4 times, notably regarding the price of nard and the cost of provisions. Luke refers to it 2 times, with the Good Samaritan entrusting two denarii to the innkeeper. John uses it in a pragmatic remark about the price of bread. Revelation cites it once in a vision of economic crisis. Everywhere, it is the currency of daily life, commerce, labor, and Roman taxation.
G1220.portee: The denarius reminds the reader that Jesus and his disciples lived in a real economy, subject to Roman authority. The parables about the denarius teach spiritual truths: God's grace surpasses our human calculations (the worker of the eleventh hour receives the same denarius), and Christian generosity must exceed monetary exchange. The denarius also symbolizes the tension between civic obligation to Rome and allegiance to God ("Render to Caesar what is Caesar's"). Finally, this concrete currency reminds us that Jesus was not detached from the material reality of his contemporaries.

sens: expresses indeterminacy or generalization: 'any', 'no matter which'
marks a concession: 'even if it were such and such'
G1221.detail:
1. This word introduces an idea of generalized indeterminacy: it means that it does not matter which one, any one. In John 5:4, the expression "whatever his disease was" indicates that healing occurred regardless of the specific nature of the ailment the sick person suffered from — it did not matter whether it was paralysis, leprosy, or another affliction.

2. This indeterminacy also carries a concessive nuance, as if saying "even if it were such a disease rather than another." The text thus emphasizes the universal effectiveness of the angelic intervention: no type of disease was excluded.
G1221.origine: The word is composed of δή (dē), an emphasis or affirmation particle, and ποτε (pote), which means 'sometimes, one day, at a moment'. Together, they form an indefinite particle that adds a generalizing force: 'any', 'whatever'. This construction is typical of Greek to express universality or indeterminacy.
G1221.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament according to the received textual witnesses, in John 5:4. It is a textual insertion present in some ancient manuscripts but absent from the most reliable ones. In this context, it qualifies the disease in a generalizing manner: regardless of the type of infirmity, healing was assured to the one who descended first into the pool after the angel's stirring. The usage emphasizes the absence of restriction or distinction.
G1221.portee: This word reminds us that in God's plan, healings are never limited to certain types of ailments or certain categories of people. Although this verse is textually debated, it invites the reader to meditate on the universality of divine compassion and the absence of discrimination in God's works.

sens: through a space or place
during a duration
by the intermediary of someone or something
because of, due to
for, with a view to
continuously, constantly
G1223.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to pass through a place. Jesus and his disciples walk "by" the fields of grain (Matthew 12:1), or traverse a region (Mark 7:31). It is the movement that crosses a boundary or traverses a space.
2. During a period of time: "by all the time of his life" (Hebrews 2:15) means throughout his existence. The word indicates the duration in which an action unfolds.
3. The idea of intermediary or instrument: something or someone through whom the action is realized. "By the prophet" (Matthew 1:22) means that God speaks through the intermediary of the prophet. "By his grace" (Galatians 1:15): grace is the means by which the divine call is transmitted.
4. The cause or reason: "why" (Luke 11:19) or "because of" (Matthew 27:18: envy is the reason for which he is delivered). It is what motivates the action.
5. The purpose or goal: to be "sent to minister" (Hebrews 1:14) expresses the destination, the intention.
6. Continuity or constant repetition: "continually" (Romans 11:10) or "always" means without interruption.
G1223.origine: This Greek word comes from an ancient root meaning "to go through," "to pass by." That is why it naturally evokes the idea of crossing, passage, intermediary. The prefix "dia-" in compound words retains this meaning: "dialogue" is to speak through another, "diameter" is the measure that passes through the center. In Hebrew, words like "min" (because of) or "be" (in, by) can be rendered by this Greek word depending on the context.
G1223.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (over 600 uses), particularly in Matthew and Paul. It is first used in the literal sense for traversing a place (Mark 2:23: walking through the fields). It can also express duration ("by all this time"). But its role as an intermediary predominates: God acts "by" Christ, "by" the prophets, "by" the Holy Spirit. Paul constantly uses it to express that everything comes from God and passes through an instrument or agent. Finally, it also expresses the cause or motive ("because of jealousy," Matthew 27:18), and sometimes the purpose or destination.
G1223.portee: This small word teaches a crucial truth of the Christian faith: God always acts through intermediaries. He speaks through the prophets, saves through Christ, builds through the Holy Spirit. Understanding this word helps to grasp that in the Bible, God's action is never isolated or arbitrary, but always mediated, mature, progressive. This also brings comfort: our prayers, our words, our actions can become instruments through which God acts for others.

sens: To take a step, to stride over
To pass from one side to the other of an obstacle (river, sea, abyss)
To go from one place to another
G1224.detail:
1. In its primary and physical sense, the word means to take a step or stride over: it is the movement of the leg that crosses a distance. The verb carries the idea of deliberate and active movement.

2. More commonly, it refers to the action of passing from one shore to another, crossing a natural obstacle: it is to cross a sea, a river, or an abyss. In Hebrews 11:29, the Israelites "cross" the Red Sea as on dry land — an act of faith that takes them from Egypt to the Promised Land.

3. In the broadest sense, the word simply expresses the action of going from one place to another, of reaching somewhere. In Acts 16:9, Paul receives the call: "Come over to Macedonia," meaning come help us over there. The word describes the movement from one region to another.
G1224.origine: The Greek word is composed of "dia" (through, by) and "baïnō" (to walk, to go). This latter root also appears in other biblical words that express movement. Together, they form the natural idea of "walking through," "going to the other side." In Acts 16:26, the impassable abyss takes up the physical idea of the word: it is an obstacle to cross that prevents any passage.
G1224.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament according to the provided usages. In Hebrews 11:29, it describes the miracle of crossing the Red Sea — not an ordinary passage, but a miraculous act where God dried up the waters. In Acts 16:9, it expresses the missionary call, the passage from one region to another for the Gospel: Paul must "cross" over to Macedonia to preach there. In Luke 16:26, Jesus speaks of an impassable abyss between the rich man and Lazarus after death — it refuses all passage, all crossing. The word thus applies to both material crossings and spiritual movements or even the impossibility of crossing.
G1224.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that faith allows us to overcome obstacles that seem insurmountable — like the waters of the Red Sea that stand before the people of Israel. It also invites us to respond to God's call to take the Gospel beyond our borders, like Paul in Macedonia. Finally, it emphasizes that there are definitive and eternal separations — some abysses cannot be crossed — which revives the urgency of salvation.

sens: To accuse someone, particularly by attacking them with malicious accusations
To file a complaint against someone with an authority
To slander, defame in an attempt to harm someone's reputation
G1225.detail:
1. The word describes the act of accusing someone, often in a malicious or false manner: it is to throw someone forward against an authority or a third party to have them condemned. In Luke 16:1, the steward is "denounced" by his adversaries as someone who wastes his master's goods — someone files a complaint against him.
2. This denunciation implies an intention to harm: one does not simply report a fact, one reports it to cause harm. The word emphasizes the malicious or false nature of the accusation: it is not just information, it is a low blow.
3. Historically, the word refers to the practice of accusing someone before an authority (a king, a magistrate) to obtain a sanction against them — a formidable weapon in palace intrigues.
G1225.origine: The word is formed from two parts: "dia-" (through) and "ballô" (to throw). The starting image is that of throwing someone across (forward), that is, delivering them, exposing them publicly to accusation. In Hebrew, it sometimes translates the verb "akhal qrats" (to devour, to tear) in contexts of false accusation. The word family includes "diabole" (slander, defamation), from which our French "diable" comes — the one who divides and accuses.
G1225.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:1, in the parable of the unjust steward. Jesus tells that a rich steward is "denounced" to his master — people file a complaint against him for wastefulness. This unique context shows that the verb applies to a specific and serious accusation, addressed to an authority (the master) to obtain their sanction. The passive used ("was denounced to him") emphasizes that the steward suffers the accusation without protection.
G1225.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of malicious accusations in human relationships. The parable highlights how denunciation can precipitate someone into disgrace, but it also invites reflection on our own integrity: the steward is denounced for his unfaithfulness. For the believer, it is a warning against lying, slander, and the desire to harm others through false accusations.

sens: To state something presenting it as certain and true
To support or defend a statement with strength and conviction
To insist on the truth or importance of what one says
G1226.detail:
1. The word means to state something in a way that presents it as certain and established. It is stronger than simply saying or speaking: it is to affirm with full certainty. In 1 Timothy 1:7, Paul describes people who assert things about the law without really understanding them — they speak with assurance, but without foundation.
2. It also means to support something with strength and conviction, to defend it against doubts or objections. The idea of "dia" (through) reinforces the intensity: one affirms in a penetrating manner, one insists. In Titus 3:8, Paul asks Titus to affirm strongly the truths of the Gospel to his people, to encourage them to act.
3. The word carries the idea of a solid affirmation, almost a guarantee. One who affirms commits themselves, asserting that it is true and important.
G1226.origine: The verb is formed from the prefix "dia" (through, with intensity) and the verb "bebaioō" (to confirm, to make stable, from which our word "bebaïos" comes, meaning firm and certain). It literally means "to affirm strongly" or "to confirm deeply." The root evokes something solid, stable, established.
G1226.emploi: This Greek verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In both cases, it involves affirming spiritual or doctrinal truths. In 1 Timothy 1:7, Paul criticizes: some assert things about the law, but they neither understand what they say nor what they affirm — it is a false assurance, dangerous. In Titus 3:8, it is Paul who commands Titus to affirm with certainty the trustworthy words of the Gospel, so that believers devote themselves to good works. In both cases, the affirmation is linked to decisive and important words.
G1226.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of what we affirm in the name of the Bible or faith. To affirm with assurance requires that we truly understand what we are saying (unlike the critics in 1 Timothy 1:7). For a spiritual leader, it is a call to declare with conviction the truths of the Gospel, not to impose, but to strengthen faith and encourage the action of believers.

sens: Look intently ahead
See with clarity and sharpness
Perceive or understand distinctly
G1227.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a gaze directed straight ahead, with concentrated attention. In Mark 8:25, the blind man healed by Jesus "looked intently" and "saw everything clearly" — this is the moment when his vision becomes clear and precise again after being blurred.
2. The word expresses the ability to see clearly, without obstacles or confusion. It is restored vision, the lucid perception of things as they truly are.
3. In a figurative and moral sense, "see clearly" means to perceive or discern the truth about oneself or others. In Matthew 7:5 and Luke 6:42, Jesus tells the hypocritical Pharisee: "then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye" — one must first remove the plank from one's own eye to see clearly the fault of another. It is to understand moral reality accurately.
G1227.origine: The word is composed of *dia* (through, over) and *blepō* (to look, to see). This composition suggests a gaze that penetrates or pierces, a look that goes beyond the surface. The basic image is that of a sharp gaze, the glance that discerns. The word family includes *blepō* (to see) and its derivatives, as well as *diablepsis* (clear vision) — the latter appears in a quotation from Aquila for Isaiah 61:1.
G1227.emploi: The verb *diablepō* appears only three times in the New Testament, all three usages being provided. Mark 8:25 uses it in the physical and literal sense: after Jesus lays hands on the blind man's eyes a second time, the man "looks intently" and regains clear and complete vision. Matthew 7:5 and Luke 6:42 (two parallel versions of the same teaching) use it in the figurative and moral sense: Jesus invites the one who has a hidden fault to see clearly their own sin before judging the sin of others. The context is always one of clear and unillusioned perception — physical in the healed blind man, spiritual and moral in the disciple called to honesty with themselves.
G1227.portee: This word reminds us that true vision — the kind that matters for our faith — first requires us to see ourselves clearly, without deluding ourselves about our own faults. It is a call to spiritual honesty: before correcting others, we must lucidly discern our own shortcomings. The word also invites trust: just as Jesus heals the blind man and allows him to "see clearly," He can open our inner eyes to the truth that sets us free.

sens: The Accuser, the one who denounces and slanders
Satan, the spiritual enemy of God and humanity
The one who sows doubt and rebellion against God
A slanderer or gossip among humans
G1228.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes one who falsely accuses, who slanders: it is a denouncer. The devil in Greek literally means "the one who throws (something) across" — the idea of separating, dividing through false accusations. John 8:44 shows this: "You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he has not stood in the truth."
2. The main sense in the Bible is Satan himself, the personal Accuser, the rebellious spirit who opposes God. Matthew 4:1-11 shows him tempting Jesus in the wilderness; Revelation 12:9 names him "the ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan." He is a spiritual being, a declared enemy.
3. The devil acts by sowing doubt, temptation, and rebellion. Luke 8:12 recounts how "the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts" — he diverts people from faith. James 4:7 commands: "Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."
4. The word can also refer to a human acting as an accuser or slanderer. 1 Timothy 3:11 exhorts women not to be "slanderers" — that is, not to play the role of the devil by sowing discord through false or malicious words.
G1228.origine: The Greek διάβολος comes from διαβάλλω ("to throw across", "to separate"). It is a compound: δια- ("through") and βάλλω ("to throw"). The original image is that of someone throwing an accusation to divide and separate. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word regularly translates שָׂטָן (Satan), whose root also means "to oppose", "to be an adversary". Both words emphasize hostility and accusation.
G1228.emploi: The word appears about 36 times in the New Testament. It almost always refers to Satan himself, particularly in the Gospels where Jesus directly confronts the devil (Matthew 4, Luke 4), and in Revelation where Satan is described in his final rebellion (Revelation 12, 20). Paul uses it to speak of the hostile spiritual power (Ephesians 6:11: "Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil"). The word also describes the agents or children of the devil: Acts 13:10 calls someone "son of the devil" because of his resistance to the truth; 1 John 3:8 asserts that "whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil." Rarely, it simply means a human slanderer or accuser (1 Timothy 3:11, Titus 2:3).
G1228.portee: Recognizing the devil as a real and organized enemy helps the believer understand their temptations and doubts: these are not merely internal weaknesses, but the actions of an active spiritual adversary. The Bible, in speaking of the devil, does not invite fear but vigilance and submission to God: "Submit yourselves therefore to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you" (James 4:7). This also means that the Christian must never act as a devil themselves, slandering or falsely accusing, but speaking the truth.

sens: Make known publicly a news, a message
Proclaim a decision or an official accomplishment
Spread the word of, widely disseminate
G1229.detail: 1. To announce something is to make it known publicly to others. Jesus tells the young man: "Go announce the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:60), meaning to go proclaim this capital news everywhere. 2. The word can also refer to the official announcement of an act or decision: Paul enters the temple to announce the day when the purification would be completed and the offering presented (Acts 21:26). 3. Finally, to announce can mean to ensure that something is known and spread to all: God says He raises Pharaoh so that His name may be "published" throughout the earth (Romans 9:17). In each case, the goal is the broad and clear transmission of a message or fact.
G1229.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "dia" (through) and the verb "aggellō" (to announce, to report), literally "to pass the word through." It expresses the idea of disseminating a message from one place to another, making it circulate publicly. This root "aggellō" is related to the messenger (an "aggelos"), the one who carries the word. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew word meaning to recount or report.
G1229.emploi: This verb appears three times in the New Testament, always with the sense of proclaiming or announcing a news. In Luke 9:60, Jesus commands the disciple to go announce the kingdom of God to all he meets. In Acts 21:26, Paul uses this verb in the sense of officially announcing an administrative or religious fact concerning purification at the temple. In Romans 9:17, the verb refers to the dissemination of God's name and power throughout the entire world. In all cases, it is about making public and widely known an important message or event.
G1229.portee: This word reminds the believer of the responsibility not to keep the message of salvation to themselves, but to make it known openly. Whether announcing the kingdom of God, a church decision, or the works of God, the Christian is called to be an announcer, someone who transmits what has been entrusted to them. It is a call to public and courageous proclamation.

sens: To pass through a period, a moment
To let time pass, to flow
To be accomplished or to come to an end (for a moment or a duration)
G1230.detail: 1. The verb expresses the idea of passing through a period or span of time: time 'flows' from one side to the other. In Acts 27:9, 'a considerable time had passed' illustrates this progression of time that moves forward and disappears. 2. When speaking of a moment that 'flows,' it emphasizes the duration that is consumed, gradually wearing away. Acts 25:13 uses the participle to indicate that 'a few days later' had passed between two events: time has silently elapsed in the meantime. 3. The word can also mean that a period comes to an end or is completed: in Mark 16:1, 'when the Sabbath was over' means that this day of rest has reached its conclusion and has disappeared. It is time that 'flows' in its course and reaches its fulfillment.
G1230.origine: The word is formed from the preposition dia ('through') and the verb ginomai ('to become, to be born'). The starting image is that of what 'becomes' by passing through a duration. It is a late verb in Greek, a poetic or Ionian way of saying that time passes and changes. It has no usage in the Greek Old Testament (only one occurrence in 2 Maccabees 11:26), which shows that it remains quite rare even in the Greek Bible.
G1230.emploi: The New Testament uses this verb only three times. Mark 16:1 uses it to express that the Sabbath has ended. Acts 25:13 and 27:9 both use it to show that time has passed between two important moments: in the first case, several days between Festus's visit to Caesarea and that of King Agrippa; in the second, a winter period when navigation in the Mediterranean becomes dangerous. The context is always one of a duration that is consumed and disappears, an interval that is crossed.
G1230.portee: This verb invites the reader to contemplate the passing of time: it reminds us that each day, each period flows and comes to an end. For the believer, this underscores the reality of time that flies and brings us closer to the day of judgment or the return of Christ. It is also an invitation not to waste the days that God gives us, but to use them wisely, knowing that time belongs to us only for a moment.

sens: To study something carefully to know its nature or truth exactly
To investigate a matter in court, weighing the evidence and arguments
G1231.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of studying attentively, scrutinizing, to arrive at precise and certain knowledge. In Acts 23:15, the Jews ask the tribune to 'examine' Paul's case, meaning to study it carefully for judgment. It is this deep knowledge, this distinction between true and false, that characterizes the word.
2. In a legal context — and this is the proper Athenian usage — 'to examine' means to conduct a trial, weighing the facts and accusations. In Acts 24:22, Governor Felix promises to 'examine' the Jews' case against Paul, meaning to know all the details and render judgment. It is the official examination of a case in court.
G1231.origine: The Greek word arises from the combination of dia ('through') and ginôskô ('to know'). This composition suggests the idea of knowing completely, reviewing, scrutinizing thoroughly. In classical Greek and Athenian law, the verb carries a precise nuance: it is the meticulous examination that a magistrate conducts before rendering judgment. The Greek Old Testament often uses it to translate the Hebrew verb 'yada,' which means to know or to recognize.
G1231.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the book of Acts, at the heart of Paul's trial in Jerusalem and Caesarea. In Acts 23:15, Paul's adversaries ask the tribune to examine his case — an examination that is actually a pretext to assassinate him. In Acts 24:22, Felix, the governor, uses the same official language: he adjourns the trial, promising to examine the case once the tribune Lysias has testified. In both cases, it is a judicial examination, meticulous and official.
G1231.portee: This word reminds us that Christian — and human — justice calls for exact knowledge, a careful study of the facts before any judgment. For the reader, it emphasizes the importance of not rushing into accusations or verdicts, but to examine carefully. It is also a lesson on fragility: even when we 'examine' a matter, the desire to harm can divert justice, as shown by the plot against Paul.

sens: The action of deciding, determining after examination
Judgment rendered by an authority
Determination of a disputed question by discernment
G1233.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of distinguishing, untangling the elements of a complex situation to grasp its true nature — it is the careful examination that precedes the conclusion.
2. In a legal context, it refers to the decision a judge renders after examining the facts and arguments: the official determination of what is just. In Acts 25:21, Paul awaits the decision of Emperor Augustus regarding his trial, meaning the judgment that will determine his fate.
3. The word also describes the discernment that allows one to decide between two positions or interpretations, penetrating to the heart of the matter.
G1233.origine: The word comes from the verb 'to distinguish' (composed of 'through' and 'to know'), which evokes the action of reviewing, examining carefully to bring clarity. This root suggests that the decision is not arbitrary: it arises from a clear knowledge of the facts, a recognition of the truth that pierces through the darkness of doubt.
G1233.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:21, in a judicial context. Paul, accused by the Jews and defending his innocence before Governor Festus, appeals to the emperor. The term 'decision' precisely designates the judgment that only Caesar can render — this verdict from above that will end the trial. The usage underscores that true decision belongs to the supreme authority, the one who has the power to know and judge definitively.
G1233.portee: This word reminds us that true decisions — those that matter for eternity — belong to God alone. Even when we find ourselves before earthly judges or tangled situations, we can entrust ourselves to the One who sees clearly and judges perfectly. It is an invitation to trust, not to resignation.

sens: to express dissatisfaction in a low voice, in a group
to manifest a muted criticism or complaint against someone
to contest or disapprove without daring to protest openly
G1234.detail:
1. The verb refers to the act of murmuring, that is, speaking in a low voice, among oneself, expressing dissatisfaction. This is typically what the Pharisees and scribes do in Luke 15:2 when Jesus welcomes sinners: they "murmured," that is, whispered their disapproval rather than confronting him directly.
2. The murmur expresses a rising criticism or complaint, often in a group. In Luke 19:7, the crowd "murmurs" because Jesus is going to eat with Zacchaeus, a sinful man: this murmur reveals the hidden judgment and resistance of the people against an action they disapprove of.
3. This murmur implies a contestation without frankness. The people who murmur disapprove but do not confide in the person targeted; they keep their complaints to themselves or exchange them with others, thus revealing a lack of trust or acceptance.
G1234.origine: The word combines the prefix "dia" (through, among) and "gogguzō" (to murmur, to produce a confused sound). The basic image is that of a murmur passing between several people, a sound of dissatisfaction exchanged from mouth to mouth. In Hebrew, this type of complaint is expressed by roots like "lin" or "lun" (to murmur, to grumble), which can be found notably in the complaints of Israel in the desert (Exodus 16:2).
G1234.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Luke, and always in the present tense to describe the murmuring of Jesus' opponents. In Luke 15:2, the Pharisees and scribes murmur against Jesus because he receives sinners. In Luke 19:7, it is the crowd that murmurs against his visit to Zacchaeus. In both cases, the murmur expresses a veiled moral disapproval, a rising criticism that remains restrained, revealing the prejudices and hidden judgment of those who cannot or dare not confront Jesus directly.
G1234.portee: This word helps us recognize that murmuring — this discreet criticism, this complaint exchanged in a group — often hides a proud judgment and a closing of the heart. The Pharisees and the crowd murmur because they cannot accept Jesus' grace towards sinners. For the Christian, this word invites us to examine whether we too murmur against God or against his intentions, rather than welcoming with confidence what he shows us.

sens: to remain aware and vigilant
to stay in a state of wakefulness despite fatigue
to remain attentive and clear-headed
G1235.detail:
1. The word describes the action of staying aware and alert, not sleeping. In Luke 9:32, Peter and his companions struggle against the sleep that overwhelms them: despite their fatigue, they manage to "stay awake" and it is precisely at that moment that they see Jesus' glory appearing with Moses and Elijah. This is the key contrast of the narrative: one must remain vigilant to see the important things of God.
2. The word also suggests the effort required to combat natural sleep, especially when one is "weighed down" (overcome by fatigue). It is not simply about being awake, but choosing to remain so, to keep one's consciousness active.
3. Figuratively, this evokes spiritual vigilance: to remain attentive and aware of God's presence, not to be numb or distracted by indifference.
G1235.origine: The word is formed from the prefix dia- ("through," "completely") added to gregoreō ("to watch," "to stay awake"). This prefix intensifies the meaning: it is not simply being awake, but truly being awake, completely. The root refers to the idea of conscious and sustained vigilance, very present in the New Testament exhortations to spiritual vigilance.
G1235.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament (Luke 9:32). It is a crucial moment in the narrative of the Transfiguration: the disciples followed Jesus up the mountain and fell asleep while Jesus was praying. When they "stay awake" (or "fully awaken"), they discover that Jesus has changed in appearance and is conversing with Moses and Elijah. The context emphasizes that this divine vision is only visible to those who remain clear-headed and vigilant.
G1235.portee: This word teaches us that the vision of God's things requires an active vigilance on our part. It is not enough to be passive or spiritually asleep: we must choose to stay awake, attentive, aware. Peter and his companions had to overcome their fatigue to see the glory of Christ. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to let the sleep of doubt, routine, or indifference prevent us from perceiving what God is doing around us.

sens: to carry through, to traverse
to let pass (time)
to live, to remain in a condition
to conduct one's existence in a certain way
to behave, to act habitually
G1236.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the verb is to carry or lead something from one point to another, to make it pass through. This is the basic image of the compound word dia- (through) and agō (to lead).

2. When it comes to time, the verb means to let days, years pass: time flows, one "traverses" it. This is where the meaning of living arises.

3. Living does not simply mean "to breathe" or "to be alive," but to lead a life, to remain in a determined condition. In 1 Timothy 2:2, we pray that believers "lead a quiet and peaceful life": the word encompasses the whole manner of living, daily existence.
