4. The verb describes how one conducts oneself, how one lives day after day: with dignity, with piety, or conversely in covetousness and envy. In Titus 3:3, Paul says that we "lived in wickedness" — this is not just existing, it is leading a life of that sort.

5. Finally, diagō emphasizes the habitual manner of behaving, the style of existence one adopts: a life of peace or a life of sin.
G1236.origine: The verb is composed of dia (through) and agō (to lead, to conduct). The basic idea is therefore "to lead through" or "to make pass through." Applied to time, which always flows, the verb comes to mean "to let flow" and ultimately "to live." It is a logically formed word: one "traverses" life by living it, day by day. It appears only twice in the New Testament, always in the sense of living or leading a life.
G1236.emploi: The verb diagō appears twice in the New Testament, only in Paul. In 1 Timothy 2:2, he asks Christians to pray for authorities, so that we may "lead a quiet and peaceful life, in all godliness and honesty": this is a harmonious and orderly life. In Titus 3:3, Paul recalls the time when Christians "lived in wickedness and envy": this is the striking contrast between what one was before and what one has become in Christ. In both cases, the word encompasses the entire existence, the habitual conduct, not an isolated moment. It is an existence that one leads from beginning to end.
G1236.portee: This verb reminds the Christian that faith is not confined to the heart or mind, but unfolds in time, in each day that we live. Praying to "lead a quiet life" means that our entire existence, our daily life, our manner of behaving with others, all of this matters. Christ transforms not only our thoughts but the way we live, how we traverse the days. It is an invitation to examine our life, our conduct, and to realign it with the Gospel.

sens: To welcome something by taking it from another, in a transmission from one generation to another
To obtain or inherit in turn what belonged to a predecessor
G1237.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of receiving something that passes from hand to hand, or from one era to another. The prefix "dia" adds the idea of passage, of succession: one does not receive first, one receives after others have had it. In Acts 7:45, the text speaks of the tabernacle that "our fathers having received" introduced into the land: it is Joshua and the following generations who inherited this sanctuary brought from the desert, and who passed it on further.
2. The word emphasizes an uninterrupted chain of transmission: what one "receives successively" is not something new, it is something accepted in continuity, with the responsibility to honor it and pass it on in turn. It is a notion of relay, of heritage, where each generation plays its role in the history of salvation.
G1237.origine: The verb is formed from the prefix "dia" (through, by succession) and "dechomai" (to receive, to welcome). This composition well expresses the notion of chain transmission: one receives not for oneself alone, but to perpetuate. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "mishné" (succession, what comes after) and "par'bar" (what passes or is transmitted). The root evokes the ancient idea of relay and generational continuity.
G1237.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:45, during Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin. Stephen retraces the history of Israel and recalls how the fathers received the tabernacle (the tent of the Covenant) and carried it in conquest of Canaan under Joshua. The context is that of fidelity to traditions and divine promises: God gave the tabernacle to Moses at Sinai, the following generations received it and continued the divine project. This rare verb emphasizes the responsible transmission from one generation to another in the economy of salvation.
G1237.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is not isolated or invented each day: it is received from one generation to another, from the apostles to the Church. Just as the ancestors faithfully carried the tabernacle, each generation of believers receives the Gospel, the Scriptures, the apostolic Tradition, with the sacred responsibility to keep them alive and to pass them on intact. It is an invitation to gratitude towards those who have gone before us, and to vigilance in our transmission.

sens: A precious band worn by the kings of Persia around the forehead or turban
Insignia of royalty and sovereign power
Crown or royal ornament worn on the head
G1238.detail:
1. The diadem is primarily a concrete object: a narrow band, often adorned with precious stones, that Persian kings would wrap around their tiara (the royal high hat) to hold it firmly in place. It is a distinctive accessory of royal dignity, visible to all who approach the monarch.
2. By its striking appearance, the diadem becomes the symbol of royal power and absolute authority. The one who wears it claims sovereignty. In Revelation, the dragon of the last times displays seven diadems on its seven heads (Revelation 12:3), thus expressing a tyrannical domination over several kingdoms.
3. The diadem also represents victorious power and legitimate authority. The risen Christ in Revelation 19:12 wears many diadems, signifying his universal kingship and his definitive triumph over all the powers of this world.
G1238.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to bind around." The diadem, literally, is what "surrounds" or "girds" the king's forehead. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "kéter" (crown), the quintessential royal insignia. Unlike "stephanos" (crown of victory or glory), the diadem specifically marks political and royal authority.
G1238.emploi: The word "diadem" appears only three times in the New Testament, exclusively in Revelation. It always denotes a visible mark of political or divine power. The monstrous dragon of Revelation wears seven (12:3), the beast coming from the sea wears ten on its horns (13:1), while the victorious Christ wears many (19:12). These three occurrences show how the diadem embodies the claim of absolute domination — whether tyrannical (dragon, beast) or legitimate (Christ). The multiplied number of diadems emphasizes the extent of this power.
G1238.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that true power belongs only to God and His Christ. The powers that display the diadem in Revelation — the dragon, the beast — usurp an authority that does not belong to them, while only Christ, bearer of many diadems, legitimately possesses universal kingship. It is a call not to fear human tyrannies, for Jesus Christ truly reigns forever.

sens: to share and give to several people
to hand out each one's share
to allocate according to needs
G1239.detail:
1. To distribute means to share something among several people, giving each one their share. Jesus "distributed" the loaves and fishes to the disciples and the crowds who were listening to him (John 6:11), like a leader who divides the spoils of war among his soldiers (Luke 11:22).
2. The word emphasizes that each one actually receives something: one does not merely show or propose, but one "hands over" to each what is due to them. In Jerusalem, the disciples made "distributions" to the widows and the poor, ensuring that everyone received according to their needs (Acts 4:35).
3. To distribute can also mean "to disperse": the spoils of the defeated are "distributed" among the victors (Luke 11:22). It is the idea of sharing and separating into parts.
G1239.origine: The Greek word συν (dia) means "through, among," and δίδωμι (didōmi) means "to give." Together, they form the image of "giving through," that is, giving by passing from one person to another, distributing. In the Hebrew of the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates חלק (halaḳ) in the sense of "to share" or "to divide." The family of the word includes διαδοχή (succession), which denotes the passage of one thing to another.
G1239.emploi: The verb απαρτίζω appears four times in the New Testament, always in the sense of "to distribute" or "to allocate." It is used in concrete contexts: Jesus distributes food to the crowd (John 6:11), Jesus commands the rich young man to distribute his goods to the poor (Luke 18:22), the early Christians distribute the proceeds of their sales to those in need (Acts 4:35). Once, it takes on the meaning of "to distribute spoils" in speaking of war booty (Luke 11:22). The word appears only in the New Testament and remains always concrete, linked to the actual sharing of goods or food.
G1239.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of sharing in the Christian community. When Jesus "distributes" the bread, he shows that the Lord generously provides for our needs. When he asks the rich young man to distribute his goods, he invites detachment and solidarity. And when the first disciples distribute the proceeds of their sales, they illustrate how the Church must concretely care for those who suffer. To distribute is not a secondary act: it is a sign of the Kingdom and of love for one's neighbor.

sens: one who comes after someone in a position, function, or dignity
G1240.detail: 1. The word designates the person who takes the place of another in an official position or power. It literally means one who "comes after" or "takes over." In Acts 24:27, Porcius Festus is the successor of Felix as Roman governor of Judea: he takes over his position and authority when Felix is recalled to Rome.
G1240.origine: The Greek word διάδοχος comes from two elements: διά ("through, after") and δέχομαι ("receive, welcome"). The basic image is that of someone who receives a function after another person, who "takes it from their hands" to continue. It is an administrative and political term, common in the Greek and Roman world to refer to magistrates and governors.
G1240.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 24:27. It is an official term to designate the governor who replaces another. Here, Festus succeeds Felix. It is a simple word, without particular nuance: it describes an administrative fact, the transfer of power from one Roman governor to his successor.
G1240.portee: This verse reminds us that earthly authorities change and that no human power is permanent. Felix, who kept Paul in prison "in the desire to please the Jews," gives way; his successor is mentioned without judgment. This shows that the course of political events serves the will of God, even if we do not immediately grasp it.

sens: To put a belt or strip of cloth around one's waist or body
To surround oneself with a garment by tying it around oneself
Figuratively, to prepare to act or to be disposed to serve
G1241.detail:
1. To gird is primarily to put a belt around one's waist to hold a garment or to don a tunic. It is a practical gesture from the ancient world: in John 13:4, Jesus "girded" himself with a cloth before washing the feet of his disciples, meaning he wrapped a cloth around his waist to serve.

2. The word also describes the state of one who is girded, dressed, and ready. In John 13:5, after Jesus girds himself with the cloth, he is described as "girded," wearing the cloth around him while he performs his service.

3. Figuratively, to gird expresses the readiness to act, to serve, or to prepare for an action. In John 21:7, Peter "girds himself" upon hearing that it is the Lord — he dresses to jump into the water, showing his eagerness to join him.
G1241.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "dia" means "around" or "through," and "zōnnumi" comes from "zōnē," the belt or girdle. The root evokes the action of surrounding, of girding. This verb often translates the Hebrew "hâgor" (to gird, girdle) in the Greek Old Testament. The image is that of a binding that encircles and holds.
G1241.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Gospel of John, around the accounts of service and revelation. In John 13:4-5, Jesus girds himself to wash the feet of the disciples — an act of humility and service that reveals his nature as a master who becomes a servant. In John 21:7, Peter girds himself upon learning of the appearance of the risen Lord — a gesture of respect and eagerness. In all three cases, the verb emphasizes a voluntary act, a preparation or an inner disposition expressed through a bodily gesture.
G1241.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, bodily gestures and clothing are never purely material: they express an inner posture. Jesus girding himself with the cloth shows us a Lord who voluntarily lowers himself to serve. When Peter girds himself to join Jesus, he manifests his love and respect. To gird is to dispose oneself, to prepare, to turn towards an action — an image for our own commitment to the Lord.

sens: Testamentary disposition, last written wishes
Agreement, convention, or arrangement between two parties
Pact established by God with His people, sealed by divine promises and conditions
G1242.detail:
1. In classical Greek, the word primarily denotes a disposition, a testament, or last wishes, meaning what a person arranges for after their death. This technical sense is seen in Galatians 3:15 and Hebrews 9:16, where Paul reasons about the validity of a written testament: a testament, once ratified, cannot be annulled or modified by anyone.

2. More broadly, it means any agreement or arrangement between two parties — a convention or contract. But in the Greek Bible, the word has taken on a particular meaning: it translates the Hebrew "berît," which designates the covenant that God makes with His people. Unlike a simple contract between equals, this covenant comes solely from God, who sets the terms.

3. The divine covenant is the heart of the story of salvation: God commits to Abraham and his descendants (Acts 7:8), then offers a new and better covenant in Jesus Christ. At the Last Supper, Jesus says: "This is my blood, the blood of the covenant" (Matthew 26:28), meaning that His death seals a new covenant, that of forgiveness offered to all peoples. The epistle to the Hebrews continually revisits this transition from the old covenant (based on the law and sacrifices) to the new covenant written in hearts (Hebrews 8:8-10, Hebrews 10:16).
G1242.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "diatithèmi" ("to dispose, arrange"), whose prefix "dia-" suggests an action that crosses over, imposed by one authority to another — hence the idea that it is God who disposes, who establishes, rather than a negotiation between equals. In translating the Hebrew "berît" (covenant), the Greek translators preferred this word over the usual term "sunthèkè" (agreement), probably because "diatèkè" better expresses God's unilateral initiative in this commitment. Related words include "diataxis" (disposition, order) and "diathesis" (arrangement, disposition of mind).
G1242.emploi: The word "covenant" appears about 30 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline epistles and the epistle to the Hebrews. The three initial senses coexist: the technical sense of testament appears mainly in Galatians 3:15-17, where Paul reasons about the validity of a testamentary disposition. But the majority of uses (28 times) refer to God's covenant with His people. Key passages recount the successive covenants: that with Abraham (Acts 7:8), that at Sinai (Romans 9:4), and especially the new covenant in Christ (Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25, 2 Corinthians 3:6). The epistle to the Hebrews extensively develops the contrast between the old covenant (often called the "Old Testament") and the new, better, and eternal one. In all cases, the covenant is the expression of God's faithfulness and grace towards His people.
G1242.portee: For the Christian, understanding the word "covenant" is crucial: it reveals that salvation is not a matter of merit or legalism, but of God's gracious commitment to us. Jesus Himself presents as the guarantor and seal of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22), one that inscribes the law in our hearts rather than on stone. This is why our two Testaments are called as such: they recount two stages of this same divine pact. Meditating on the covenant anchors us in the certainty that God keeps His promises and calls us to respond with faith and obedience.

sens: Distinction ou différence entre choses
Division ou distribution de choses en plusieurs parts
Variété de dons, de ministères ou d'opérations spirituelles
G1243.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a distinction or difference between several things: it is the fact that things are not identical, but separate and distinct from one another.
2. It then signifies a division or distribution, as when sharing something into several portions: each part receives its own function or role.
3. In its biblical usage, the word especially expresses the variety or multiplicity of spiritual gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, Paul enumerates the "diversities" of gifts, ministries, and operations: there are many different gifts, many different ways to serve, many different effects of divine power, but they all come from the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God.
G1243.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "dia" (through, separation) and the verb "hairein" (to take, to seize), hence the verb "diairein" (to divide, to separate into parts). The Hebrew word it translates in the Greek Old Testament is "makhlokèth," which means division or separation. The root thus evokes the idea of separating, dividing into distinct portions.
G1243.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6. Paul uses it to speak of the spiritual gifts that the Holy Spirit distributes to believers: diversity of gifts in verse 4, diversity of ministries in verse 5, diversity of operations in verse 6. In this context, the word does not emphasize confusion or discord, but rather harmony in diversity: despite the differences in functions and effects, all come from the same divine source. It is a diversity that is intentional and ordered.
G1243.portee: This word teaches the believer that the Church is not uniformity, but richness in variety. Each person receives different gifts, different callings, and this is a strength, not a weakness. We must accept and value the diversity of ministries rather than fear or envy it; it all comes from the same Spirit and pursues the same goal: the edification of the body of Christ.

sens: Diviser quelque chose en parts distinctes
Répartir entre plusieurs personnes
Donner à chacun sa portion
G1244.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of dividing a whole into separate pieces or parts: it is to cut, to share what was whole. In Luke 15:12, the father "divides" his property, that is, he divides it among his sons so that each receives his share.
2. To distribute then means to allocate these parts among different people, giving each what is due to them. In 1 Corinthians 12:11, it is the Spirit who "distributes" spiritual gifts to each believer according to His own will.
3. The word thus evokes the idea of a fair and orderly distribution: it is not about throwing randomly, but giving each their portion, based on an intention or authority (the father, the Spirit).
G1244.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "dia-" (through, between) combined with "aireō" (to take, to seize). The original image is that of "taking while separating," sharing what one holds. The root describes the action of dividing and distributing simultaneously. It is a verb of sharing and distribution that implies an authority distributing the good.
G1244.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament according to the Segond. In Luke 15:12 (the parable of the prodigal son), the father distributes his inheritance among his sons, each receiving their share. In 1 Corinthians 12:11, Paul uses it to show that the Holy Spirit distributes the charisms (spiritual gifts) to each member of the body of Christ according to His sovereign will. In both cases, the verb emphasizes that the distribution is a voluntary and thoughtful action, not arbitrary: it belongs to a benevolent authority.
G1244.portee: This word reminds the Christian that all good comes from God and that its distribution follows a wise plan. Seeing that the Spirit "distributes" gifts to each according to His will invites us to accept the role assigned to us and to honor the gifts of others, without jealousy or envy. It is also an invitation to share generously what God entrusts to us.

sens: Démontrer l'erreur ou le mensonge de quelqu'un par des preuves irrécusables
Confondre quelqu'un en montrant que sa position n'est pas fondée
G1246.detail:
1. To refute is to prove that a statement is false by providing solid evidence. In Acts 18:28, Apollos refutes the Jews by relying on the Scriptures: he does not merely contradict them, he demonstrates through the biblical text that Jesus is the Christ. It is a complete and definitive refutation that silences the one who is mistaken.
2. The word also denotes the action of confounding someone in front of witnesses, particularly in public. Apollos refutes the Jews "publicly": everyone sees that his evidence is solid and that his opponents have no response. It is a victory of truth over error, visible and recognizable.
G1246.origine: The Greek word combines three elements: "dia-" (through, all the way), "kata-" (downward, completely) and "elegchos" (refutation, conviction). These particles intensify the action: one does not refute halfway, one refutes thoroughly. The word "elegchos" primarily denotes the proof that confounds the opponent, the irresistible argument. The root evokes the action of bringing to light, of unveiling the lie through demonstration.
G1246.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:28. Apollos, presented as "an eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures," refutes the Jews who oppose the Christian message. He acts publicly and relies on the written text. The context shows that refutation is a key element of Christian preaching: not only to announce the faith, but also to demonstrate that it is rooted in biblical revelation and that unbelief has no foundation.
G1246.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Christian faith is not a vague feeling, but a conviction based on evidence. It also invites clarity and rigor in testimony: when proclaiming the Gospel, one can show that objections to faith carry no weight against the Word of God. It is a model for those who wish to defend and explain their faith intelligently.

sens: To render service to someone, to help them concretely in their daily needs
To wait at table, to serve meals
To exercise the function of deacon in the Christian assembly
To serve a cause, to accomplish a mission in service of an ideal
To provide, to make available for common utility
G1247.detail:
1. The most common meaning is to render service, that is, to help someone by meeting their concrete needs. Jesus says in Luke 22:27: "I am among you as one who serves," showing that true service is a humble attitude, available, and oriented towards others.
2. A specific usage concerns service at the table: bringing food, preparing meals for guests. In Luke 8:3, women "provided for him out of their means," supplying what was necessary; in Matthew 8:15, Peter's mother-in-law "served" him (probably by preparing his meals).
3. The verb also designates the office of deacon, one who helps the assembly. In 1 Timothy 3:13, those who "serve well as deacons" gain "great confidence in the faith."
4. More broadly, to serve means to dedicate oneself to a cause, to accompany a mission. In Romans 15:25, Paul says he is going to Jerusalem "to serve the saints," that is, to support the poor Christians.
5. In a passive sense (especially in 2 Corinthians 3:3 and 8:19-20), the verb can mean to be provided, supplied, put into action for a common purpose.
G1247.origine: The word comes from the Greek διάκονος (diakonos), which designates one who serves. This root evokes the image of a person who bends down, who lowers themselves to serve — the idea of humble availability. In classical Greek, it was sometimes associated with simple service tasks. The Hebrew word that this Greek verb often translates is שׁרת (shérath), which also means to serve, but in the sense of service in the Temple or in the service of a king. This family of words (diakonos, deacon, diaconate) has traversed the entire Christian history since its origins.
G1247.emploi: This verb appears 32 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. The Gospels use it to describe service at the table and concrete human service: Jesus washes the feet of the disciples, the angels "serve" Jesus in the desert (Matthew 4:11, Mark 1:13). Paul uses the word in an ecclesial sense, speaking of the tasks of deacons (1 Timothy 3:10, 13) and the help provided to brothers in distress (Romans 15:25). Peter's epistles use it to urge Christians to "serve" one another in love (1 Peter 4:10, 11). The meaning evolves slightly: from concrete and daily service to the mission of the Church, but the spirit remains the same: selflessness and availability.
G1247.portee: This word invites the believer to see service as a central virtue of the Christian life, not as a chore. Jesus himself took the form of a servant, and he teaches that greatness in the Kingdom comes from the willingness to serve others — the small, the sick, the poor. For the Christian, "to serve" is not a humiliation but an honor and a path to freedom: it is by turning towards others that one finds true greatness.

sens: Domestic service, work in service of a household
Action of serving at table or taking care of someone's well-being
Mission or function exercised in service of the Church
Pastoral charge or function of spiritual responsibility
Material aid and assistance provided to those in need
Accomplishment of a task entrusted by God
G1248.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of domestic service: it is the daily work in service of a household. Martha exemplifies this well in Luke 10:40, where she is busy with "domestic tasks" while her sister sits at Jesus' feet. It is the work of a servant.

2. By extension, it is the action of serving at table or taking care of the well-being of others. The word always retains this flavor of humility and devotion: one puts oneself at the service of someone else.

3. In the epistles, the word takes on a spiritual significance: it designates the mission or function exercised in service of the Church. In Romans 12:7, Paul speaks of "ministry" as a calling to which one is called and to which one must "adhere."

4. It is also the pastoral charge or the function of spiritual responsibility exercised by elders and church leaders. Titus is tasked with "fulfilling" his ministry (2 Timothy 4:5), and Paul himself praises his apostolic charge (Romans 11:13).

5. The word also applies to material aid and assistance provided to those in need. In Acts 11:29, the Church sends "aid" to the brothers in Judea during the famine. It is a concrete act of charity.

6. Finally, it is the accomplishment of a task or function entrusted by God: Paul speaks of the "ministry of the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:8) and the "ministry of reconciliation" (2 Corinthians 5:18), showing that all true ministry is a work of God.
G1248.origine: The word comes from "diakonos" (servant, deacon), which originally designates one who serves at table or who performs humble service. The root "dia" (through) and "koneo" (to become dusty, to make efforts) paints the image of a service activity that requires effort. In the Greek Old Testament, "diakonia" often translates Hebrew words meaning "service" or "office." The word has retained its concrete meaning of service while taking on, in the New Testament, an ecclesial sense: ministry becomes the service of God and His Church.
G1248.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles. In Luke and Acts, it sometimes retains its meaning of domestic service or material aid (Luke 10:40; Acts 11:29). But in Paul, it massively designates spiritual ministry: the apostolic function (Romans 11:13), the charge of deacon (Romans 12:7), the ecclesiastical office (Ephesians 4:12, Colossians 4:17). Paul also uses the word in a figurative sense: "ministry of death" (2 Corinthians 3:7), "ministry of the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:8), "ministry of reconciliation" (2 Corinthians 5:18), to describe the spiritual work itself. In the pastoral epistles (1 and 2 Timothy), he qualifies Timothy's charge as pastor (2 Timothy 4:5). In Hebrews and Revelation, it even applies to angels and the work of Christ.
G1248.portee: This word reminds Christians that all true ministry is first and foremost a humble service, in the image of Jesus who washed the feet of his disciples. It invites everyone to recognize their particular calling: whether it is pastoral, apostolic, or a simple help to brothers, it is ministry as long as it is offered to God. The word also teaches that Christian service is never a career or power, but a charge given by God to build His Church and assist the weak.

sens: One who fulfills a service role for a person or community
One who serves Christ or the Gospel
One who holds an officially recognized position in the Church, a deacon
One who performs a task in service of a cause
One who voluntarily places themselves under the authority of someone else
G1249.detail:
1. Generally, a servant is one who performs a task for someone else, an aide or assistant. In the Gospel, Jesus uses this word to describe one who wants to be great: "Whoever wants to be great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:26). It is a relationship of service towards a person or group.

2. A servant of Christ or God is one who dedicates their life to serving the Lord and His cause. Paul refers to himself: "I am a minister of Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:23), and he speaks of those who serve Christ faithfully (Colossians 1:7).

3. A deacon (deaconess in the feminine form) is an officer of the Church, recognized and ordained for a ministry of service within the Christian community. The technical term appears in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8 to designate a specific role in the early Church.

4. This word can also describe one who acts in service of a task or work, such as the magistrate who is "God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:4), exercising authority as an instrument of divine purpose.

5. The word also suggests a voluntary attitude of submission and humility: one who freely takes the posture of a servant in the Kingdom of God.
G1249.origine: The etymology of the Greek word is uncertain. In Hebrew, it primarily translates נַעַר (young man, young servant) and שָׁרַת (to serve). The Greek word διάκονος is distinguished from δοῦλος (slave) and θεράπων (voluntary servant) because it primarily considers one who dedicates themselves to a task or function rather than mere personal obedience. Unlike λειτουργός (which emphasizes service rendered to the community), διάκονος focuses on the execution of the service itself.
G1249.emploi: This word appears 28 times in the New Testament. It is absent from the Gospel of Luke and infrequent in John (where it is found for the servants at the wedding at Cana, John 2:5, 9). Paul uses it abundantly to speak of himself and his collaborators (2 Corinthians 3:6, 6:4, 11:23; Colossians 1:7, 1:23, 1:25). In the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, it is used to illustrate the humility required in the Kingdom (Matthew 20:26, 22:13, 23:11; Mark 9:35, 10:43). The technical sense of "deacon" appears in the Pastoral Epistles (1 Timothy 3:8, 3:12) and in Philippians (Philippians 1:1). The context shows that the Christian servant does not submit because of a lower status, but out of commitment to the cause of Christ.
G1249.portee: For the Christian, this word redefines greatness according to the Gospel: to be great is to serve. It challenges our relationship to power and authority — every role in the Church is primarily a service, not a power. It also calls to recognize that serving God or serving Christ is a noble vocation, not a degradation. Finally, it teaches that the Christian is indebted to God and others for their actions.

sens: The number 200
G1250.detail: 1. This word simply expresses the number 200, composed of two hundreds. It appears in very concrete contexts of daily life: Jesus asks His disciples if it would take "two hundred denarii" worth of bread to feed the crowd (Mark 6:37), or Philip estimates the cost of insufficient provisions at "two hundred denarii" (John 6:7). It is also found to measure distances — the boat was about "two hundred cubits" from the shore (John 21:8) — or to count men — Paul has "two hundred soldiers" assembled (Acts 23:23) and the ship carried "two hundred seventy-six people" (Acts 27:37). In John's vision, the two witnesses prophesy for "one thousand two hundred sixty days" (Revelation 11:3).

sens: To listen to a case as a judge
To give an official hearing to someone to hear their defense
G1251.detail:
1. This verb designates the action of listening to a judicial matter in a complete and authoritative manner. The prefix "dia" (through) intensifies the idea: one truly listens, all the way through, examining the case carefully. It is the technical verb for a magistrate who presides over a hearing. In Acts 23:35, Governor Festus tells Paul: "I will hear you when your accusers arrive," which means he will grant an official hearing and listen to the accusations and the defense.
2. By extension, it is the action of summoning someone and giving them the opportunity to speak in their defense before a court. This implies a voluntary act by the magistrate who recognizes the accused's right to be heard.
G1251.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "dia" (through, completely) and the verb "akouō" (to listen, to hear). This composition reinforces the simple meaning: instead of hearing vaguely, one hears "through" or "all the way to the end." In Hebrew, the underlying verb is "šāma'" (to hear), which in legal contexts also carries the idea of an official hearing. The word belongs to the family of verbal communication verbs in Greek.
G1251.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:35. It is a technical term from Roman judicial vocabulary, used when Festus, the governor of Judea, assures Paul that he will bring him before him to hear his case. The context is one of legal protection: Paul, imprisoned and accused, receives assurance that he will have the right to a fair hearing. This precise judicial vocabulary shows that Luke, the author of Acts, is attentive to the details of Roman legal procedures.
G1251.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian faith unfolds in the real world, including in the face of civil authorities. The assurance that Paul receives — to be heard judicially — illustrates how God protects His servants through human institutions, even imperfect ones. For any Christian facing injustice, this passage highlights the importance of the right to be heard and the role of civil justice.

sens: Separate, distinguish, recognize differences
Judge, arbitrate, decide a matter
Hesitate, doubt, be divided in mind
G1252.detail:
1. To discern primarily means to mentally separate in order to clearly see the differences. When Jesus says that one can "discern the appearance of the sky" (Matthew 16:3), He is speaking of this ability to observe and distinguish signs. Similarly, Paul asks: "who makes you different?" (1 Corinthians 4:7), meaning who has separated you from others by giving you particular qualities.
2. To discern also means to judge, arbitrate, make a decision. When Paul writes, "If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged" (1 Corinthians 11:31), he invites everyone to examine and judge their own conduct. This is the sense of judgment as discernment of good and evil.
3. In the sense of hesitating, the word expresses being torn between two thoughts, without assurance. "Without hesitation" (Acts 10:20) means without doubt or indecision. When one "doubts" (James 1:6; Romans 14:23), one is divided within oneself, believing and not believing at the same time.
G1252.origine: The Greek word διακρίνω (diakrinō) is composed of δια (dia, "through") and κρίνω (krinō, "to separate, to judge"). The basic image is that of dividing, separating into two. The root κρίνω refers to the action of sifting or discerning. In the Old Testament, this verb translates Hebrew words such as שׁפט (šāphat, "to judge") and דִּין (dîn, "to regulate, to arbitrate"), which share this idea of distinguishing the right from the wrong.
G1252.emploi: Διακρίνω appears 18 times in the New Testament, primarily in Acts, the letters of Paul, and James. The two meanings are intertwined: to discern (distinguish) and to doubt (hesitate). In the Gospels and Acts, it often refers to discerning signs, differences, or spirits. In Paul, we find the meaning of "to judge" in the context of Christian discipline (1 Corinthians 11:31) and the meaning of "to doubt" when lacking faith (Romans 4:20; 14:23). In James, "to doubt" is related to the instability of one who does not firmly believe (James 1:6; 2:4). Jude uses it for dispute and contention (Jude 1:9, 1:22), showing how doubt becomes quarrel.
G1252.portee: Understanding this word helps the believer on two levels. First, to discern requires cultivating the ability to see clearly, to judge reality healthily (Matthew 16:3). Second, the word warns against doubt and hesitation: to doubt within oneself is to be divided, without an anchor of faith. Jesus and Paul invite a trust without reservation, as shown by the prohibition against doubting in requests made to God (Matthew 21:21).

sens: Judgment that distinguishes and evaluates
Ability to untangle what is good from what is bad
Spiritual gift of discerning spirits
Skill acquired through experience and practice
G1253.detail:
1. Discernment is the act of judgment by which one evaluates and distinguishes things — separating them to understand. In Romans 14:1, Paul speaks of not "quarreling over opinions," meaning not to judge others' convictions on subjects where each must form their own judgment.
2. It is a moral faculty: the ability to recognize what is right from what is wrong. In Hebrews 5:14, the author describes those "whose judgment is exercised by use to discern good and evil," as a skill that develops through training and practice.
3. It is also a gift of the Holy Spirit in 1 Corinthians 12:10: "the discernment of spirits" is among the charisms, that is, the supernatural abilities that the Spirit distributes to believers for the edification of the assembly — here, the special gift of recognizing true spirits from false ones.
G1253.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « diakrínô » (διακρίνω), which literally means "to judge through" or "to separate": dia (through) + krínô (to judge, to decide). The basic image is that of a separation or fine distinction. It is a compound word that expresses the idea of sifting, untangling. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew « miphlash », which also refers to a discriminating thought, a judgment.
G1253.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. In Romans 14:1, "opinion" refers to personal convictions on which weak believers should be accepted without judgment. In 1 Corinthians 12:10, the "discernment of spirits" is a charism — a gift of the Spirit to test spirits (see also 1 John 4:1) and distinguish what comes from God from what does not. In Hebrews 5:14, the meaning is that of a trained moral aptitude, an experience that sharpens judgment. The three uses share the idea of distinguishing and evaluating, but in different contexts: judgment of people, supernatural judgment, moral judgment.
G1253.portee: This word shows the believer that discernment is a grace to cultivate. It is both a gift of the Holy Spirit and a skill that develops through use and maturity: one is not born with discernment, one forms it. It is also a weapon against hasty judgment of others and a defense against spiritual seduction — knowing how to discern what is good helps protect the faith of the assembly.

sens: Hinder someone, resist them
Refuse consent to an action
G1254.detail:
1. To hinder someone, to resist them: this is the concrete meaning of the word, which designates an action or a word that blocks another person's path. It is like putting a barrier or a dam in front of someone who wants to move forward.
2. To refuse consent to an action: this is the most common application in the Bible. In Matthew 3:14, John opposes the baptism of Jesus — he does not want it to happen and he clearly states it. It is a motivated refusal, which manifests a conviction or an objection.
G1254.origine: The word comes from the Greek root κωλύω (kolúō), "to prevent, to stop," with the prefix δια (dia), "through." This composition reinforces the meaning: it is to prevent decisively, by blocking the passage. The prefix dia suggests an action that crosses or divides. This word often translates the Hebrew verb לבל (lbil) in the Greek Old Testament, which carries the same idea of obstacle or refusal.
G1254.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 3:14, during the baptism of Jesus. John the Baptist opposes Jesus' plan: he feels his unworthiness and expresses his objection. The context shows that opposing Jesus is a natural reaction in the face of the superiority of One recognized as the Messiah. This unique appearance in the New Testament makes this moment particularly significant.
G1254.portee: The word shows us that John the Baptist was right to feel a barrier between himself and Jesus, but that Jesus wanted to overcome this objection to fulfill His mission. This teaches that sometimes, even our rightful reservations must yield to God's purposes, and that obedience to His will takes precedence over our feelings of unworthiness.

sens: to speak together about something
to discuss among themselves to decide on an action
G1255.detail:
1. To converse means to have a conversation, to exchange words with someone about a topic. It is to speak together, often to share what one thinks or what one has learned. In Luke 1:65, after the birth of John the Baptist, the people of the hills of Judea "were conversing" about all these wonderful events: they were talking to one another, amazed by what had happened.
2. To converse can also mean to discuss together to make a decision, to deliberate together on the course of action to take. In Luke 6:11, the Pharisees "consulted" to know what they would do to Jesus: filled with fury, they spoke among themselves to decide how to act against him.
G1255.origine: The word comes from a composition: the prefix "dia" (through) joins the verb "lalèô" (to speak, to say). The starting image is that of a word that crosses, that passes from one person to another — hence the natural idea of conversing, of exchanging words. This Greek formation is well rendered in French by "s'entretenir" or "consult" depending on the context: a word that circulates among several.
G1255.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke, the evangelist who depicts the reactions of the crowds. In Luke 1:65, he describes how the news of the birth of John the Baptist spreads in hearts and on lips: the people "were conversing" about these wonderful things. In Luke 6:11, it is a deliberation: the Pharisees "consulted" together about what they would do to Jesus. The word thus carries two close nuances: sometimes an admiring conversation that is shared, sometimes a discussion where one reflects on an action to be taken.
G1255.portee: This verb shows us how words and thoughts spread among people: either in wonder and sharing of what God does, or in malice and plotting against him. It invites us to examine the content and spirit of our own conversations: do we speak to praise the works of God, or to conspire against him and his servants?

sens: To have a conversation, an exchange of words with someone
To discuss a topic, to debate it
To teach, to convey a teaching through words
To dispute, to seek to convince through argumentation
G1256.detail:
1. The simplest meaning is that of an ordinary conversation: to have a dialogue, to converse with someone. This is what Paul does in Ephesus, "entering the synagogue, he conversed with the Jews" (Acts 18:19). The idea is that of a natural and direct exchange of words.
2. To converse can also mean to discuss a specific topic, to examine it together. When Paul "spoke about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment" before Felix (Acts 24:25), he was not just talking, but developing a theme, an argument.
3. The word takes on a pedagogical shade: to teach, to communicate knowledge or truth. After having difficulty convincing, Paul "taught daily in the school of a certain Tyrannus" (Acts 19:9), thus marking a shift to regular instruction.
4. In debates and quarrels, to converse becomes to dispute, to seek to convince the opponent. On the way, the disciples "had discussed among themselves who was the greatest" (Mark 9:34), mixing discussion with rivalry.
G1256.origine: The word comes from the Greek διαλέγω, composed of "dia" (through, mutually) and " légô" (to speak, to say). The basic image is therefore that of words passing from one to another, a dialogue where each says something. In the Greek Old Testament, the verb often translated the Hebrew "dibber" (to speak) in the intensive mode, especially in contexts where God speaks with power or where one discusses a matter firmly.
G1256.emploi: The verb appears mainly in the Acts of the Apostles (about 10 occurrences), rarely elsewhere. It describes Paul's missionary activity: conversing with the Jews in the synagogues (Acts 17:17; 18:4, 19), conversing with converts (Acts 20:7), teaching in a school (Acts 19:9). It is also found in the context of a long instruction or preaching (Acts 20:9, where Paul's "discourse" lasts so long that a young man falls asleep). Mark 9:34 uses it for a dispute among disciples, Hebrews 12:5 for an exhortative discourse, Jude 1:9 for a contention. The tone varies: simple conversation, serious debate, structured teaching, or quarrel.
G1256.portee: This word shows how the Good News spread: not from above, imposed, but through dialogue, patient conversation, the exchange of ideas. Paul does not shout his convictions; he converses, he discusses, he teaches day after day. For the Christian, this reminds us of the importance of conversing seriously about the things of God, not shying away from sincere questions, and understanding that sharing faith often happens in the intimacy of a true conversation.

sens: To temporarily stop an action
To take a break, to leave an interval
To discontinue a gesture or attitude
G1257.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of stopping something, but not definitively: it is an interruption, a pause. In Luke 7:45, the sinful woman "has not ceased" kissing Jesus' feet: she stopped intermittently, but she continued, unlike Peter who only gave her a single kiss.
2. The image is that of a break or an interval in a continuous action. The word evokes less a complete stop than discontinuity, a momentary absence.
3. In this passage, the contrast is striking: while Peter gave a single kiss upon arrival, this woman maintained her gesture of tenderness without interruption — she did not "cease," she left no interval.
G1257.origine: The word is formed from δια (through, intermittently) and λείπω (to leave, to abandon). This composition suggests the idea of "leaving by intervals." The root λείπω is found in other biblical words such as ἐλλείπω (to fall short, to lack). In ancient Hebrew, the word יחל sometimes translates this notion of interruption or temporary cessation.
G1257.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 7:45. It occurs in this crucial moment where Jesus compares the behavior of Simon the Pharisee with that of a woman recognized as sinful. Simon did not give Jesus the expected gestures of hospitality (water for the feet, kiss of welcome), while this woman has not ceased to kiss his feet since her arrival — her demonstration of repentance and love has been continuous and generous.
G1257.portee: This passage teaches that true love for Jesus is manifested by perseverance and continuity, not by the superficial gestures of conventional politeness. The woman who "has not ceased" shows a heartfelt fidelity that Simon, in his unbelief, cannot understand. For the believer, this reminds us that the relationship with God is not measured by appearances, but by the constancy of the heart.

sens: Language or dialect of a people, region
Particular way of speaking characteristic of a community
Oral expression in a specific language
G1258.detail:
1. The word designates the spoken language of a people or region — not the physical organ, but the system of communication that characterizes it. At Pentecost, each person hears "in their own language" (Acts 2:6, 8): the pilgrims gathered in Jerusalem recognize their native dialect, the one they speak at home.
2. It is also the distinctive way of speaking of a community. When Paul "speaks in the Hebrew language" (Acts 21:40, 22:2, 26:14), he adopts the dialect that his listeners — the authorities and disciples of Jerusalem — understand and respect. It is a concrete choice, related to whom one is addressing.
3. The word can designate a specific named language: Jesus and Paul speak "in the Hebrew language," that is, in Aramaic (the Hebrew dialect spoken at the time). It is never a mysterious or unintelligible word, but a real language, understood by those who master it.
G1258.origine: The word comes from the verb "dialégomai" which means "to discuss, converse by sharing words." The root "dia-" (through) + "lektos" (spoken) evokes the idea of a word that crosses, that is transmitted from one person to another. In the Greek Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew "lashôn" (language), which designates both the organ and the language it produces. The Greek word initially meant "conversation," then specialized to designate the language or dialect characteristic of a place or people.
G1258.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, only in Acts, to describe the languages spoken in Jerusalem at the time of Pentecost and during Paul's testimonies. At Pentecost (Acts 2:6, 8), it marks astonishment: each hears the message "in their own language," that of their childhood and region — a miracle of communication that abolishes linguistic barriers. When Paul testifies (Acts 21:40, 22:2, 26:14), he deliberately chooses to speak in "the Hebrew language" to be heard and listened to by his brothers: it is a strategy of welcome and respect. In Jerusalem (Acts 1:19), the field of blood bears a name "in the language" of the local people. The word always emphasizes the concrete and relational dimension of language: one speaks to be understood, and the choice of language creates a bond or an obstacle.
G1258.portee: This word reminds us that authentic communication requires respect for the one being addressed: Paul does not impose his language, he adopts that of his listeners. For the Christian reader, it is a lesson in pastoral wisdom: sharing the Gospel also means seeking to be understood, to adapt the message to the language of the listener. The diversity of languages, far from being a curse, becomes at Pentecost the sign of God's power that transcends boundaries: a single message, heard by each in their own language, reveals that the Holy Spirit addresses everyone, without exception.

sens: change hostility into friendship
restore a broken relationship between two people
make peace after a conflict
G1259.detail:
1. The word paints the image of hostility transforming: instead of enmity, friendship is born. It is a complete change of disposition. In Matthew 5:24, Jesus commands the believer to "be reconciled" with their brother before presenting their offering at the altar — an urgent and necessary reconciliation.
2. More concretely, it is to restore a broken relationship, to make the rupture between two people disappear. The word suggests that both parties must move, mutually consenting to peace.
G1259.origine: The Greek word combines "dia" (through, mutually) and "allassō" (to change, exchange). It thus evokes a change that occurs on both sides. The image is one of mutual transformation: both enemies change their hostility into friendship together. It is a richer term than others that mean reconciliation, as it emphasizes the reciprocity and mutual concession that true peace requires.
G1259.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 5:24, where Jesus teaches reconciliation as an absolute moral priority. Before even approaching God with an offering, the believer must first be reconciled with the one they have offended or who has offended them. The passive use of the verb ("be reconciled") marks the action of the one who accepts to seek peace and change their heart towards their neighbor.
G1259.portee: This word reminds us that reconciliation is not an optional suggestion, but a command at the very heart of the Gospel. It requires an active personal initiative — not just waiting for the other to take the first steps. It places peace with one's neighbor on the same level as the worship of God: it is impossible to serve the Lord as long as the breach with a brother is not healed.

sens: Weigh the pros and cons, deliberate internally
Think, reflect silently
Question oneself, wonder
Discuss among several people
G1260.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to weigh reasons, to deliberate: this is what happens in Matthew 21:25 where the chief priests reflect on how to respond to Jesus — they weigh the consequences of each answer. 2. More broadly, it is to think, to turn a question over in one's mind: Mark 2:8 says that the scribes "thought" within themselves what they did not say out loud. 3. It is also to wonder, to question oneself internally: Luke 3:15 shows the people who "were wondering" if John was the Messiah — a question that rises silently from the heart. 4. When several people exchange their thoughts in this way, the verb takes on the meaning of discussing: Mark 8:16 recounts that the disciples "reasoned" among themselves about the lack of bread.
G1260.origine: The word comes from two elements: "dia" (through, in two opposite directions) and "logizesthai" (to count, calculate, weigh). The image is one of calculation, of balance — one puts the reasons on one side and the other to see which prevails. It is a verb that the Greeks used for accounts and political deliberations. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb "hashab," which has the same meaning of counting, meditating, thinking.
G1260.emploi: The verb appears 15 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke). It almost always describes the inner thoughts of the disciples or crowds: how they react to Jesus, what they imagine, what they wonder. Jesus himself sometimes uses it to show that he knows their hidden thoughts (Mark 2:8, Luke 5:22). The verb is often used with complements indicating the solitude of this thought ("within themselves") or the exchange ("among themselves"). The verb never describes a large public discussion: it is always a silent reflection or a low-voiced conversation.
G1260.portee: This verb reminds us that Jesus sees beyond words — he knows the inner reasoning, doubts, and hidden calculations of the heart. For the reader, it invites us to take our secret thoughts seriously: what we ruminate alone or among friends does not escape God's gaze. It also pushes us to examine our own deliberation — do we really weigh our choices in the light of faith, or only according to our interests?

sens: movement of the mind that reflects, reasons, or doubts
content of thought: idea, opinion, or conviction
hidden intention, secret calculation
inner questioning, hesitation
judgment or evaluation one makes about something
G1261.detail:
1. Thought is primarily the internal work of the mind that reflects and reasons. It is the act of thinking, the movement by which one weighs a question, deliberates. Jesus "knew their thoughts" (Luke 6:8): he perceived this internal work of the disciples who were questioning him.

2. It is also the content of this work: the idea, opinion, conviction that results from it. "Out of the heart come evil thoughts" (Matthew 15:19) lists the intentions and resolutions that arise within us.

3. Thought can be a hidden intention, a calculation, or a secret aim, often malevolent. In Romans 14:1, welcoming someone without "judging their thoughts" means not condemning them for their personal choices.

4. It is also the movement of doubt, hesitation that arises in the heart. "Why do these thoughts arise in your hearts?" Jesus asks the frightened disciples (Luke 24:38): he points to their anxious questioning.

5. Finally, thought is the judgment one forms, the appreciation one makes: "The thoughts of the wise" (1 Corinthians 3:20) are their reasonings, their conclusions.
G1261.origine: The Greek word dialogismos comes from the verb dialogizesthai ("to reason, deliberate") composed of dia- ("through, separation") and logos ("word, reason"). It thus designates the work of reason that traverses the mind, separating and evaluating. In Hebrew, it often translates machshavah ("thought, plan"), which comes from a root meaning "to weave, to frame," as one weaves an intention. The word evokes both conscious deliberation and secret calculation, visible thoughts and hidden intentions.
G1261.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (especially Luke) and in Paul's epistles. In Luke, it often appears when Jesus "knows the thoughts" of the disciples or the scribes (Luke 5:22, 6:8, 9:47): Jesus reveals what is happening in the heart, internally. In Matthew and Mark, it concerns the "evil thoughts" that come from the human heart and pollute it. In Paul (Romans 1:21, 1 Corinthians 3:20), it refers to human reasoning separated from God or considered by God: the "vain" thoughts of the wise. In 1 Timothy 2:8 and Philippians 2:14, thought is what stirs the inner self and creates quarrels. It is always something intimate, that remains in the heart until it is "unveiled."
G1261.portee: This word teaches us that God knows our most secret thoughts, those we hide even from ourselves. It calls us to vigilance: where do our thoughts come from? Are they aligned with the Word of God or lost in doubt and calculation? It also invites us to seek the purity of heart, for what we think in secret shapes our actions and our character.

sens: to disperse, to dissolve (referring to a group of people)
to be routed, to be defeated
G1262.detail:
1. The word describes the action of separating and dispersing. When a united group dissolves, its members disperse in different directions like an assembly that dislocates. This is what happened to the disciples of Theudas: after his death, his four hundred followers were dispersed and ceased to constitute an organized force (Acts 5:36).
2. It also means to be routed or defeated, like an army that loses the battle and whose soldiers flee. Dispersion is not just a material fact; it is also the collapse of a cause or movement.
G1262.origine: The word comes from the preposition "dia" (through) and the verb "luō" (to loosen, detach, dissolve). The basic image is that of something coming undone, disintegrating, loosening from within. That is why "dialuō" evokes both physical dispersion and the collapse of a structure or organized movement.
G1262.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:36. Peter uses it to describe what happened to the movement led by Theudas: after the death of its leader, all who had followed him were routed and reduced to nothing. It is a typical example of the rapid downfall of a false messiah and his movement: human organization collapses when its foundation is not solid.
G1262.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the fragility of human movements that do not rely on God. The implicit contrast is instructive: the movement of Jesus, unlike that of Theudas, survived the death of its master precisely because it was founded on the resurrection and the power of the Holy Spirit. The dispersion of Theudas' followers shows that a cause without divine foundation cannot endure.

sens: to testify officially and urgently
to affirm something insistently and gravely
to adjure someone by invoking divine authority
to announce a truth while committing oneself personally
G1263.detail:
1. To solemnly attest: this means to testify not just simply, but with force and authority, as Peter and John do after miraculous healings (Acts 8:25). The testimony is not an opinion; it is a committed assertion.

2. To affirm insistently: the word carries the idea of pressure, persuasion. Paul does this to the Jews in Corinth (Acts 18:5): he does not merely preach; he strongly emphasizes each point to convince them that Jesus is the Messiah.

3. To adjure, to conjure: when the context is solemn or submitted to God, the word takes on this shade. Paul adjures Timothy "before God" (1 Timothy 5:21) — it imposes an obligation by invoking the weight of divine presence.

4. To announce while committing oneself: with Paul again (Acts 20:24), announcing the grace of God is not just speaking: it is doing so at the cost of one’s life, which makes his attestation total and true.
G1263.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition *dia* (through, completely) joined to *marturomai* (to testify, to bear witness). This composition reinforces the simple meaning: it is not an ordinary testimony, but an intensified testimony that traverses, that penetrates. The root word *martus* means "witness" and comes from a judicial context. In Hebrew, the verb *ʿûd* (to testify) in the intensive form produces the analogous idea of supported and repeated testimony.
G1263.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts and the pastoral epistles. Peter and John use it after miracles (Acts 8:25), Paul in Corinth when he preaches to the Jews (Acts 18:5), and later before the elders of Ephesus (Acts 20:21, 23, 24). The verb often appears in a context of missionary proclamation: bearing witness to the resurrection, to grace, to the kingdom. In Paul, *diamarturomai* is often accompanied by personal intensity: he commits his life, his integrity. In the epistles to Timothy, the context becomes that of solemn adjuration, almost judicial — Paul adjures Timothy before God and the angels (1 Timothy 5:21, 2 Timothy 2:14, 4:1). The meaning nuances according to the context: public attestation in Acts, solemn charge in the epistles.
G1263.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that testimony is not enough: it is *engaged* testimony that the Church needs. The apostles do not recount the facts with detachment; they engage themselves, they take weight upon their shoulders. It is an invitation not to fear to speak one’s faith clearly, solemnly, putting one’s life at stake — just as Paul says: to finish one’s race with joy (Acts 20:24). For a Christian, it is both a permission and a call to testify not timidly, but with full awareness and complete conviction.

sens: struggle, combat
vigorous dispute, argument
G1264.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes a fight or struggle, an action of battling against someone or something — the image is one of intense physical or moral opposition.

2. Specifically, when it comes to words, it is a lively dispute, an unreserved contestation. In Acts 23:9, during Paul's trial, the Pharisees "engaged in a lively debate": they stood up to vigorously contest the accusations against the apostle, asserting that they found no fault in him.
G1264.origine: The word is composed of the preposition dia- ("through," "entirely") and the verb machomai ("to fight," "to struggle"). This composition reinforces the idea of intense and sustained struggle. In Hebrew, this verb often conveys the word for "to fight" or "to battle" (root lhm), expressing a determined opposition.
G1264.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 23:9). It denotes the passionate debate that erupts during Paul's trial before the Sanhedrin: some Pharisees, upon hearing Paul speak of the resurrection of the dead, rise to energetically defend him against the Sadducees. The context shows a vigorous altercation, marked by conviction and liveliness of tone, rather than a mere polite discussion.
G1264.portee: This word reminds us that faith can provoke serious debates and unreserved positions. In Paul's case, the lively debate that arises becomes an opportunity for the Gospel to be heard and to divide minds according to the truth — an opposition that testifies that the message matters and touches consciences.

sens: To stay in a state or condition without moving or changing
To persevere, to hold firm in the face of opposition or difficulty
To subsist, to continue to exist over time
To keep something intact, to preserve it
G1265.detail:
1. To remain silent: this means to stay in a state of silence, without speaking (Luke 1:22). The word evokes permanence, a persistence in a given condition.
2. To persevere with someone in trials (Luke 22:28): this means to stand firm by their side, not to abandon them despite difficulties. This perseverance is a form of moral constancy.
3. To subsist, to continue to exist (Hebrews 1:11): Christ persists eternally while all things pass away. It conveys the idea of durability and permanence in the face of destruction.
4. To maintain the truth intact (Galatians 2:5): this means to preserve something in its integrity, not allowing it to erode or become compromised. Everything remains as well (2 Peter 3:4): the world persists in its current state.
G1265.origine: The Greek word διαμένω is composed of δια ("through") and μένω ("to remain, to dwell"). This combination reinforces the idea of permanence and continuation. The root μένω is itself fundamental in Greek and appears in many compounds. In Hebrew, the verb עמד ("to stand, to subsist") often conveys this nuance of solidity and persistence.
G1265.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, spread across the Gospels, Paul's epistles, and the Catholic epistles. In Luke, it first describes a physical state (to remain silent) and a moral attitude (to persevere in trials). Paul uses it to defend the integrity of the Gospel truth against pressures. The epistle to the Hebrews uses it to contrast the eternity of Christ with the vanity of creatures. Finally, 2 Peter applies it to the permanence of the present world. The meaning thus varies according to the context: physical state, perseverance, eternity, or continuity of the cosmos.
G1265.portee: This word reminds us that Christian truth, like Christ himself, subsists and persists in the face of the assaults of time and opposition. It also invites the believer to perseverance: to remain faithful in faith and trials, without being diverted from the Gospel. It is a word of stability and encouragement for those who doubt or are weary.

sens: To divide an asset among several people by distributing it
To allocate or give each their share
Separation of a group into opposing or hostile parts
G1266.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to divide an asset or object into parts and give it to several. This is what happens to Jesus' clothes during the crucifixion: the soldiers "share" them among themselves by casting lots (Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24). It is also to distribute to each their portion, as Jesus shares the cup at the Last Supper: "distribute it among yourselves" (Luke 22:17).
2. The word also describes the action of distributing something, particularly when each takes or receives their share. At Pentecost, the first Christians "share" their goods among all according to needs (Acts 2:45).
3. On a spiritual and social level, it means to be separated, divided in convictions or loyalties. Jesus declares that his coming will "divide" families: "five in one house will be divided, three against two" (Luke 12:52-53). This evokes a rupture, an opposition among members of the same group.
G1266.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix "dia-" (through, in two, on either side) and the verb "merizō" (to share, to divide), which itself comes from "meros" (part, portion). In the Greek Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew "halaq" (to share, to divide). The basic image is one of separation: to divide something for distribution, or to separate elements that were united.
G1266.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the New Testament. It first expresses the material action of sharing goods: Christ's clothing (4 passages), food among believers (Acts 2:45). It also carries the meaning of "to divide" in contexts of conflict or disunion: Jesus asserts that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand (Luke 11:17-18), and his coming will create division in families (Luke 12:52-53). The word can be in the passive (to be shared, to be divided) or in the middle (to share among oneself). Its biblical usage always emphasizes a distribution or separation with real consequences.
G1266.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus was stripped down to his clothes for our salvation: nothing was spared from him. It also shows us the spiritual cost of following Jesus: far from superficially uniting, the Gospel provokes a clarification of true alliances. Finally, the sharing of goods among believers is not a theory: it is a concrete practice of the first century, a driver of authentic unity.

sens: Separation, rupture between people or groups
State of discord and conflict within a community
G1267.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a clear separation, a rupture between distinct people or groups. It is the opposite of unity and communion. In Luke 12:51, Jesus explicitly contrasts it with peace ("Do you think that I have come to bring peace on earth? No... but division"), showing that this term evokes a deep fracture.
2. More broadly, it describes the state of conflict, discord, and disagreement that prevails when people are divided. Division is not merely a geographical or administrative separation, but a relational rupture: it creates tension, disagreement, and even hostility among those it affects. In the context of Luke 12, Jesus warns that his teaching will provoke this division, even within families.
G1267.origine: The Greek word comes from the root διαμερίζω (diamerizō), which means "to divide, to share." The prefix διά- expresses separation "through," and μέρος (meros) means "part." It is a compound word that emphasizes a division into several parts, a marked rupture. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it translates notably מַחֲלֹקֶת (makhlōqeth), which also evokes division, discord, or conflictual sharing.
G1267.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 12:51. Jesus uses it in a discourse about his messianic role: he did not come to bring peace in the human sense, but rather an inevitable separation between those who follow him and those who reject him. This division even cuts through families, as Jesus mentions elsewhere that he will come to "set a father against his son" (Luke 12:53). The context shows that this division is a spiritual consequence of the Gospel: it reveals hearts and forces a choice between following Jesus or remaining attached to the values of the world.
G1267.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that the Gospel is not a simple social or personal improvement, but a call that transforms relationships and provokes decisive choices. Following Jesus can be costly, even in the closest ties. This does not mean that Christians should intentionally create conflict, but rather that they should not be surprised if their faith disturbs or separates. It is a call to clarity and faithfulness, even in the face of misunderstanding.

sens: To spread, to diffuse in space or among people
To become known, to circulate (a rumor, news)
G1268.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of dispersing, gradually spreading: something spreads like poured water. In Acts 4:17, the religious leaders fear that the news of Jesus' resurrection will spread among all the people, like a rumor that gains more and more ears.
2. By extension, "to spread" means to become known and propagated: information diffuses, circulates, reaching an increasingly broad audience. The verb emphasizes less the voluntary action than the natural process of expansion.
G1268.origine: The word comes from the preposition "dia" (through, by means of) and the verb "nemō" (to distribute, to divide, to share). This composition suggests the idea of sharing something by distributing it widely, hence the meaning of spreading or dispersing. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate the Hebrew verb "halaq" (to divide, to share). The word emphasizes less the deliberate action than the process of dissemination.
G1268.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 4:17, where it is used in the passive voice ("to be spread"). Peter and John have just healed a lame man and spoken publicly in the name of Jesus; the religious authorities, worried, decide to forbid the apostles from continuing, for fear that the news of this miracle will permeate the entire population. The context shows that this word describes the propagation of information, a word, or news that extends irresistibly. The passive use suggests that the authorities cannot stop this natural process of diffusion.
G1268.portee: This word reminds us that the word of God and the Gospel spread naturally, almost despite obstacles: it cannot be confined or contained. It invites the believer to recognize the expansive power of the message of the Resurrection and to understand that human will cannot prevent God from making Himself known.

sens: To express something by a gesture of the face or hand, without words
To communicate an idea or intention through mimicry
To manifest something to someone through a movement of the body
G1269.detail:
1. To make a sign is to communicate through a visible gesture — a wink, a nod, a hand gesture — rather than by words. It is a body language, immediate and often discreet. In Luke 1:22, Zechariah, rendered mute after his vision in the temple, "made signs" to tell what he had seen: he used his whole body to convey his message since his voice was taken from him.
2. This gesture can be a simple indication, a call, an attempt to catch someone's attention. It implies an intention to communicate something specific — not a mere meaningless movement, but a gesture that conveys meaning.
G1269.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "dia" (through, by) and "neuō" (to make a sign, to nod, to point). The root "neuō" expresses the idea of a movement of the neck or head. It is a word that depicts the concrete gesture by which one attracts attention silently. In the Greek Old Testament, it sometimes translates the Hebrew "qrts," which means to wink or make a mocking gesture with the eyes.
G1269.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in Luke 1:22. It describes Zechariah the priest who, having received a vision from the angel Gabriel in the temple, finds himself unable to speak. When he returns home, he cannot tell his family and neighbors what happened; so he communicates through gestures — he "made signs" to them. This context shows the word in its full sense: a means of non-verbal communication, an expressive gesture compensating for the absence of voice.
G1269.portee: This word reminds us that human communication does not always pass through words. Even rendered mute, Zechariah can convey the seriousness and reality of his divine encounter. It also speaks to us of patience and attention: those around him understood the message; they read his gestures. In our faith life, this encourages us to recognize that God also communicates through other means than words — through signs, circumstances, gestures.

sens: Movement of the mind that conceives an idea, an intention
What occupies the mind, what one thinks intimately
G1270.detail:
1. A thought is the inner movement by which the mind conceives an idea or forms an intention. In Luke 11:17, when the text says that Jesus "knew their thoughts," it refers to the secret intentions that the disciples keep within themselves — what they really think about Jesus and what he says.
2. More broadly, this word designates what occupies a person's mind, their inner calculations, their personal reflections. It is the content of consciousness, what forms in the heart before manifesting in words or actions.
G1270.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to think" or "to reflect" (διανοέομαι). The prefix "dia-" (through) suggests a thought that traverses or crosses the mind. In Hebrew, there is a related notion with the word מַחֲשָׁבָה (machshavah), which also means "thought" or "plan." This Greek term belongs to the family of words that describe the mental and spiritual activity of consciousness.
G1270.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:17. Jesus uses it to refer to the hidden thoughts of those who follow him — what is really happening in their hearts and minds, beyond what they express aloud. The context shows that Jesus, in his divine insight, penetrates not only the words but also the intimate intentions and secret calculations of those around him. This word emphasizes the depth of the Lord's knowledge.
G1270.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus knows not only our actions and words but also our innermost thoughts, what happens in the secret of our hearts. It is both an invitation to spiritual sincerity and a call to keep our thoughts oriented towards him, knowing that they cannot be hidden from his infinite wisdom.

sens: The faculty of understanding and reflecting
The activity of the mind that conceives intentions and plans
Concrete thoughts, the ideas we form
The dispositions of the heart revealed by thought
The spiritual heart where God inscribes His law
G1271.detail:
1. Thought is the faculty of the mind that understands, judges, and reflects. It is intelligence in action, capable of grasping the truth. Jesus asks us to love God "with all our mind" (Matthew 22:37), which means to engage our entire capacity to understand and desire what is good.

2. Thought also refers to the intentions and plans we form internally. These are the movements of the mind that direct our actions. Colossians 1:21 speaks of evil thoughts that separated us from God: these are the hostile or selfish intentions we harbor.

3. Specifically, these are particular thoughts, the ideas we conceive at a given moment. Luke 1:51 mentions the "proud thoughts" that people carry in their hearts: imaginations of grandeur, selfish calculations.

4. Thought reveals what truly inhabits the heart, our true moral and spiritual dispositions. In Ephesians 2:3, our thoughts and desires show that we are "children of wrath" before grace.

5. Thought is also the spiritual seat where God writes His law and will. Hebrews 10:16 promises that God will put His laws "in the heart and in the mind": thought becomes the place of knowledge and obedience to God.
G1271.origine: The word comes from the verb "to think" (dia = through, and noein = to perceive by the mind).
