It originally designates the movement of the mind that traverses, that penetrates to understand. In Hebrew, it often translates the word "heart" (leb or lebab), because in biblical thought, it is in the heart that reflection, will, and intentions reside, long before it designates the physical organ. Thought is therefore never purely intellectual: it is inseparable from feelings and moral dispositions.
G1271.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles. In the Synoptics, it appears in Jesus' words asking for total love for God (Matthew 22:37, Mark 12:30, Luke 10:27, echoing Deuteronomy). In the Pauline and Petrine epistles, thought becomes the object of a spiritual transformation: God wants to renew our thoughts (Ephesians 4:18), reconcile us by changing what we think of Him (Colossians 1:21), or inscribe His law in them (Hebrews 8:10, 10:16). In 2 Peter 3:1, having a "pure mind" is a call to vigilance in faith. The word thus shows a progression: from simple mental faculty to the issue of inner conversion.
G1271.portee: This word reminds us that for God, it is our thoughts that truly matter. To love God "with all our mind" means that it is not enough to do good out of habit: we must engage our heart and mind. Thought reveals who we truly are, and that is why God wants to transform it. Recognizing that our thoughts separate us from Him (Colossians 1:21) and accepting that He renews them (Ephesians 4:18) is the very heart of the Christian conversion.

sens: To completely open a door, an entrance, the eyes, the heavens
To access understanding, the intelligence of something
To explain, clarify the meaning of a text or a word
To prepare the heart to understand and receive
G1272.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to open what was closed. When Jesus says "Ephphatha, be opened" (Mark 7:34), He commands the opening of the deaf man's ears. The eyes of the disciples are opened and they recognize the risen Jesus (Luke 24:31). The heavens are opened in a vision (Acts 7:56). It is a complete, definitive act: the word suggests an action that moves from a closed state to an open state.
2. The word also applies to the mind or understanding. Jesus "opens" the minds of the disciples so that they can understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45): He makes them capable of grasping what they could not see before. It is to make transparent, to make readable what was obscure.
3. To open also means to explain, to develop the meaning of a text. When the disciples say "He was explaining the Scriptures to us" (Luke 24:32), the verb "to open" expresses how Jesus unfolds, details, brings to light what the Scriptures contain. It is to give access to the hidden meaning.
4. Finally, the word can describe the opening of the heart to faith. Lydia is said to have had "her heart opened" to listen (Acts 16:14): she was willing, ready to receive. It is an inner opening, a readiness.
G1272.origine: The Greek word δι-αν-οίγω combines three elements: "dia" (through), "ana" (upward, again) and "oigō" (to open). This composition suggests a complete, in-depth opening that traverses. In Hebrew and Aramaic, verbs like פָּתַח (patach, to open) or פָּקַח (paqach, to open the eyes) are used in the Greek translation to render this term. The image is one of passage: what was closed becomes accessible.
G1272.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, almost always in Luke. It first designates concrete physical acts: healing the deaf by opening his ears (Mark 7:34), recognizing the risen one when the eyes are opened (Luke 24:31), seeing the heavens opened (Acts 7:56). But very quickly the word shifts towards the spiritual and intellectual: opening the mind to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), explaining the Scriptures by opening them before the disciples (Luke 24:32, Acts 17:3), opening the heart to receive the word (Acts 16:14). Luke uses this word to show how, through Jesus or the Spirit, what was inaccessible or closed becomes clear and received. Physical opening becomes the sign and figure of spiritual opening.
G1272.portee: This word speaks to the believer of liberation and access. It suggests that faith is not an isolated effort, but a received opening: it is the eyes that Jesus opens, it is the mind that He opens, it is the heart that He prepares. This encourages both prayer (asking Jesus to open our eyes) and obedience (welcoming this opening when it comes). The word also teaches that understanding Scripture is not purely a human task, but an action of God: we need Him to open our minds.

sens: To spend an entire night from one place to another or in one place
To spend the night in prayer, in vigilance
G1273.detail:
1. The word designates the action of crossing or experiencing an entire night. It is the time that passes from evening to morning, but the word emphasizes the act of actively traversing it, of accomplishing it. In Luke 6:12, Jesus "spent the whole night praying to God": He did not sleep, but remained active during those dark hours.
2. In particular, spending the night in prayer or vigilance means performing an important action during the night hours. The usage in Luke 6:12 shows Jesus spending an entire night in prayer on the mountain before choosing His twelve apostles: it is a time of intense communion with God, without rest.
G1273.origine: The word is formed from the prefix διά (through) and νυκτερεύω (to spend the night, from the Greek νύξ, "night"). The basic idea is to cross or pass through the night. The prefix διά reinforces the idea of duration and totality: the whole night, from beginning to end. In classical Greek, this verb is infrequent; in the New Testament, it appears only once.
G1273.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:12, where it describes Jesus spending the whole night praying before a decisive moment in His ministry. In the Greek Old Testament, the verb appears in Job 2:9, where it describes Job spending the night in a situation of trial. In Luke 6:12, the context shows that this night of prayer was an act of intense communion with God, preceding the crucial choice of the twelve apostles. The use of the verb emphasizes not only that Jesus slept little, but that He remained engaged in spiritual activity until morning.
G1273.portee: This word reminds us that prayer can require time and perseverance, even during hours when rest would be natural. The example of Jesus spending an entire night in prayer before His major decisions teaches the believer that important moments of discernment and communion with God may demand total dedication. It is an invitation to take our relationship with God seriously, without counting the cost.

sens: To fully accomplish, finish a journey or action
To continue a journey to its end
G1274.detail:
1. The word means to finish something by fully accomplishing it: it is to complete what one has undertaken. In Acts 21:7, Paul and his companions "complete" their sailing from Tyre to Ptolemais — they finish the journey by arriving at their destination.
2. By extension, it also means to continue a journey or action to the end, to persevere until the finish. The idea is one of a journey brought to completion: one does not stop along the way, but goes all the way through.
G1274.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "dia" (through) and the verb "nuō" (to accomplish, to finish). This composition suggests the idea of both crossing and finishing: one goes beyond obstacles to achieve their goal. The word belongs to classical and late Greek, used notably by early Christian writers to describe the accomplishment or continuation of an action.
G1274.emploi: The verb appears only once in Acts 21:7, in the account of Paul's journey to Jerusalem. Paul and his companions leave Tyre by boat and "complete" their sailing by arriving at Ptolemais. The context shows that the word applies to the completion of a maritime journey: to finish a trip successfully. It is a rare word in the New Testament, expressing the idea of perseverance to the end.
G1274.portee: This verb invites the reader to reflect on faithfulness and perseverance: Paul completes his journey despite dangers and obstacles. For the Christian, it is a reminder that faith requires not giving up along the way, but pursuing until the fulfillment of what God entrusts to us, just as Paul perseveres in his mission until Jerusalem.

sens: to pass from one side to the other, to cross a distance
specifically, to cross a body of water, a sea
to go from one place to another by overcoming an obstacle
G1276.detail:
1. The word primarily means to cross, that is, to pass from one bank or side to the other. It is the action of overcoming space to reach the opposite side. Jesus and his disciples "cross" the sea by boat (Matthew 9:1).
2. In most biblical uses, the word specifically describes the crossing of a sea or a large body of water. After "crossing" the sea, the disciples arrive in the land of Gennesaret (Matthew 14:34; Mark 6:53).
3. The meaning can broaden to any transition from one place to another, even figuratively: in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, it speaks of those who would like to "cross" the chasm that separates heaven from hell (Luke 16:26).
G1276.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: dia- ("through") and peraō ("to pass, to cross"). The underlying image is that of passage, of crossing. The root "pera" literally means "the other side," and the verb expresses the action of going to that "other side." In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew ‹ ābar ›, which carries the same idea of passage and crossing.
G1276.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament, almost always to describe a maritime crossing. Jesus and his disciples do this regularly on the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 9:1; 14:34; Mark 5:21; 6:53). The usage is very concrete: it involves real passages from one bank to another. Only the occurrence in the parable of the rich man (Luke 16:26) uses the word figuratively, to speak of an insurmountable limit between two worlds. In Acts 21:2, it is a ship that makes the "crossing" to Phoenicia. The word remains invariably linked to the idea of passing from one space to another by overcoming a distance or an obstacle.
G1276.portee: This word reminds us that material obstacles—a sea, a distance—can be overcome by faith and obedience. The disciples do not fear the crossing because Jesus is with them. But it also tells us that there are absolute limits that no one can surpass: eternal fate cannot be changed after death (Luke 16:26). It is an invitation to take our present choices seriously.

sens: To cross the sea by boat
To cover a maritime distance
To progress in a journey by sea
G1277.detail:
1. To cross the sea by boat, passing from one shore to another or through a well-defined maritime area. The word evokes the concrete action of sailing on water with a ship to reach a destination. In Acts 27:5, Paul and his companions "navigate through" the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia during their journey to Rome, which shows the context of a maritime crossing with defined stages.
2. More broadly, to progress or advance in a maritime journey by crossing bodies of water. This is the sense of continuous and deliberate movement through maritime areas, especially when connecting several coastal regions.
3. In a figurative sense (as in Greek philosophers), to navigate the course of life as one crosses the sea — that is, to face the trials and challenges of earthly travel. This poetic image compares human existence to a navigation fraught with obstacles.
G1277.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "dia" (through) and "pleō" (to navigate, to sail). This root "pleō" evokes the image of the ship's movement on the water. The composition "dia-" + "pleō" creates a sense of crossing or passage through a maritime area. This verb belongs to the vocabulary of navigation and maritime travel in ancient Greek.
G1277.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:5, during the detailed account of Paul's journey to Rome. It is a key moment in Paul's missionary journey: the ship, with its prisoners and soldiers, crosses specific maritime areas (Cilicia and Pamphylia) on the way to a later destination. The context is that of real and observable navigation, without figurative meaning. This tumultuous journey, which will lead to shipwreck, is narrated with concrete and precise terms.
G1277.portee: This word reminds the reader that even the journeys of the apostles were real and dangerous physical trials. Paul did not preach comfortably: he faced the perils of the sea, storms, and uncertainty. This underscores the determination and concrete commitment of the early Christians in the mission of evangelization, at the cost of material suffering.

sens: to be exhausted or worn out by prolonged effort
to be irritated or dissatisfied
G1278.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes physical or mental fatigue due to intense work: one is worn out, exhausted by what demands a lot of effort. Paul, harassed for days by the possessed girl in Acts 16:18, ends up being "tired" — not only of this situation but of the spirit that torments her. It is after this accumulated fatigue that he turns around and casts out the spirit in the name of Jesus.
2. The word also takes on the meaning of deep irritation or dissatisfaction that comes from this weariness. The Jewish leaders in Acts 4:2 are "dissatisfied" that Peter and John are teaching the resurrection: their annoyance arises from an opposition that troubles and wears them down morally. The same Greek root "pon-" that speaks of effort and work also expresses this emotional disturbance.
G1278.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "dia-" (through, beyond) and "poneō" (to work, to toil). The starting image is that of a fatigue that permeates the whole being, that completely traverses it — hence the intensity of the weariness. In the Greek translators of the Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew "atsab" (to toil, to grieve), showing that biblical fatigue is never purely physical: it also affects the soul.
G1278.emploi: The verb appears twice in Acts and nowhere else in biblical Greek. In Acts 4:2, it describes the irritation of the religious authorities in response to the apostolic announcement — a moral and spiritual disturbance. In Acts 16:18, it designates Paul's real fatigue, exhausted by the repeated harassment of the slave girl before he commands the spirit to leave her. The context shows that even the apostles experience real human limits: they become tired, they are irritated, but they act nonetheless by the power of the Holy Spirit.
G1278.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life unfolds in a real body, with its strengths and limits. Paul does not cast out the demon out of impatience or selfishness: his accumulated fatigue is honest and understandable. Similarly, being upset or dissatisfied in the face of opposition to the Gospel is not a spiritual flaw — it is a just human reaction. The text teaches us that God does not despise our fatigue: He knows it and acts despite it, by His grace.

sens: To pass from one side to the other, to cross a space
To move through a place, to traverse
To go from one place to another by passing through intermediate locations
G1279.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of crossing or traversing a physical space: Jesus "was crossing" fields of grain (Luke 6:1), passing directly through them. The image is one of movement going from one side to the other.
2. The word also designates the act of traveling or traversing a region: Jesus "was crossing" towns and villages while teaching (Luke 13:22), meaning He was passing through these places successively to go elsewhere.
3. In a more abstract usage, it simply means to pass by someone or to review: the crowd that "passes by" (Luke 18:36) is the crowd that circulates, going from one place to another. Paul hopes to see you "in passing" (Romans 15:24) when he travels to Spain, meaning stopping briefly at your place on his way.
G1279.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "dia" (through) and the verb "poreuō" (to go, to move). It literally means "to go through." In Hebrew, it often translates verbs like "to go" or "to pass" (עָבַר, הָלַךְ). The prefix "dia" emphasizes the idea of crossing or passing from one side to another.
G1279.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Luke and once in Paul. It describes the movement of Jesus and His disciples through regions (Luke 6:1, 13:22) or the passing of a crowd (Luke 18:36). In Acts, Paul "passes" through towns to convey the decisions of the assembly (Acts 16:4). The word is often used without a direct object (absol.) simply to mean "to pass" or "to go." It always evokes a movement that crosses or traverses a space, whether geographical or temporal.
G1279.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus was in constant motion, going from place to place to announce the kingdom. It also shows that the apostles did not remain confined but "passed" to strengthen and instruct the assemblies. For the believer, this teaches that faith is not static: it is carried and communicated on the way, in the everyday of our movements and encounters.

sens: to be completely disoriented, not knowing how to react
to be troubled by something strange or unexpected
to be plunged into uncertainty and mental confusion
G1280.detail:
1. To be completely disoriented, not knowing how to react. It is the state of one who faces a disconcerting event and cannot find their bearings: the mind falters. Herod heard about Jesus and His miracles, but he did not know what to think — too many contradictory versions circulated about His identity (Luke 9:7).
2. To be troubled by something strange or unexpected. When something escapes ordinary understanding, one enters into this perplexity. At Pentecost, after the supernatural signs and Peter's preaching, the crowd was astonished and did not know what to think of this miracle (Acts 2:12).
3. To be plunged into uncertainty and mental confusion. It is a state where one goes around in circles, unable to settle on an explanation. The chief priests, learning of the boldness of the imprisoned apostles who preached freely, did not know what to think — no threat seemed to stop these men (Acts 5:24; Acts 10:17 for Peter with his vision).
G1280.origine: The word combines the prefix dia- ("through," the idea of crossing or difficulty) with the verb poreō which means "to be without resources," "to be short of ideas." The starting image is that of someone crossing a mental dead end, who cannot find a clear path: thoughts intertwine without finding an exit. This deep confusion characterizes the moment when the event exceeds ordinary categories.
G1280.emploi: The verb appears only four times in the New Testament, always in the form that means "to be perplexed." Luke uses it twice (Luke 9:7 for Herod; Acts 10:17 for Peter), and Luke also reports it twice in Acts (Acts 2:12 after Pentecost; Acts 5:24 in the face of the apostles' imprisonment). Each time, the author describes the mental shock provoked by something extraordinary — a miracle, an announced resurrection, a vision from heaven, superhuman boldness. It is always a moment when ordinary reason is insufficient.
G1280.portee: This word helps the reader recognize true moments of spiritual crisis, where God acts beyond what was expected. Herod, the crowd of Jerusalem, Peter himself — all had to let their certainties be disturbed. Perplexity is not a lack of faith; it is often a sign that one is facing the true action of God, which forces us to revise our ideas. It is a call to humility of thought.

sens: to produce a profit, a capital gain
to make fruitful a entrusted asset
to obtain a beneficial result through work or trade
G1281.detail:
1. The word designates the action of making a sum of money produce a profit, as when it is invested to yield returns. In the parable of the talents in Luke 19:15, the master asks his servants how each has made the entrusted money "worthwhile": he wants to know what profit they have derived from their management.
2. More broadly, it refers to making fruitful, taking advantage of an asset or responsibility so that it bears fruit. The image is that of wealth being put to work, growing and multiplying through trade or effort.
3. The term also carries the idea of accountability: not only making the asset profitable but also demonstrating, accrediting, justifying it through concrete results.
G1281.origine: The Greek word combines a prefix that intensifies the action with a root meaning "to negotiate" or "to deal with a matter." This root evokes commerce and exchange, hence the natural idea of making a profit. In late Greek, this compound verb specialized in the commercial and financial sense: to make money work to yield a gain.
G1281.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:15. Jesus uses it in the parable of the king who departs and entrusts money to his servants. The context is that of stewardship and responsibility: each servant must account for how he has made the capital entrusted to him "worthwhile" (or neglected it). The word emphasizes that managing assets is not neutral: one should expect fruit, an increase.
G1281.portee: This word from Jesus challenges every Christian regarding how they manage what has been entrusted to them—talents, time, resources, spiritual gifts. "Making worthwhile" is not hoarding out of fear or letting one's abilities lie dormant: it is accepting a responsibility for growth and service. The master's judgment rests on concrete results, reminding us that our life with God is not solely contemplative but productive.

sens: To be filled with an inner rage that drives one to act
To feel a rage so intense that it consumes the heart
G1282.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of an inner rage that accumulates, as if one is being sawed from the inside. In Acts 5:33, when the apostles proclaim that Jesus is the Savior, their adversaries become furious—a rage so intense that it immediately drives them to want to kill them.
2. This fury reaches the heart itself and manifests physically. In Acts 7:54, Stephen recounts to the Jewish leaders what God has shown him; they are furious in their hearts, to the point that they grind their teeth against him—an image of rage that invades the whole being and seeks to express itself through violence.
G1282.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "dia" (through) and "priō" (to saw, to cut). The basic image is that of a saw cutting through something—hence "to saw in two." Used in the passive and figuratively, it describes a rage that cuts through you like a blade, tearing you apart from the inside. It is a vivid and expressive word, from popular rather than scholarly language.
G1282.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Acts, and always to express the fury of the enemies of the Gospel. In Acts 5:33, it arises when the proclamation of the risen Jesus is heard. In Acts 7:54, it rises when Stephen recalls the people's refusals to listen to God. In both cases, this fury is immediate, visceral, directed against those who testify of Christ. It is a word for moments of crisis, when anger causes one to lose control.
G1282.portee: This word reveals how the Gospel provokes a radical reaction: either the acceptance of grace or violent rejection. It also shows that the fury of adversaries is proportional to the certainty of those who proclaim Christ. For the Christian, it is a reminder that witnessing to the Gospel can provoke visceral opposition—not out of personal hatred, but because the Gospel touches the heart in the most sensitive places.

sens: To take and carry away the belongings of a person by force or plunder
To strip someone of their possessions
To destroy by removing wealth
G1283.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to take and carry away the belongings of a person, usually by force or violence. This is what a raider or organized thief does: he empties a house of its riches. In Matthew 12:29 and Mark 3:27, one cannot plunder the house of a strong man unless he first overpowers him.
2. It is also the action of stripping someone of all their possessions, violently depriving them of their goods. The verb implies violence, systematic plunder, far beyond simple theft.
3. Figuratively, the verb can mean to destroy or weaken by removing what constitutes strength or wealth. Jesus uses the image to speak of one who would have the power necessary to plunder the goods of the devil.
G1283.origine: The word is composed of the prefix διά (dia, "through") which intensifies the action, and the verb ἁρπάζω (harpazō, "to seize, to take away by force"). This root ἁρπάζω evokes the brutal action of snatching something away. The corresponding verb in the Old Testament Hebrew was בָּזַז (bazaz) and גָּזַל (gazal), both meaning to steal or plunder violently.
G1283.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in two parallel passages: Matthew 12:29 and Mark 3:27. In both cases, Jesus speaks in parable of someone entering the house of a strong man. He explains that it is impossible to plunder his goods without first binding that strong man. The context is that of the battle against the devil and the deliverance of the possessed: Jesus asserts that one must first defeat the prince of darkness before being able to take away those he holds under his power.
G1283.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that Jesus speaks as one who has the power to defeat Satan. The image of plundering the goods of the defeated enemy reminds us that Christ's victory is not nominal: it produces concrete fruits, the deliverance of captives. It also encourages the believer not to underestimate the power of the defeated enemy, but to recognize that this victory has been won by the one who is stronger.

sens: To break or split a soft object (fabric, net) by pulling forcefully
To break or shatter what holds or binds
To express intense emotion through this gesture: pain, indignation, shock
G1284.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: it is to tear or split something violently. A net breaks under the weight of fish (Luke 5:6), chains yield under the strength of a demoniac (Luke 8:29).

2. For bonds and chains, the verb describes the moment when what holds gives way, breaking cleanly, freeing what was imprisoned. It is a forced rupture, not a simple release.

3. When speaking of clothing, tearing takes on an expressive dimension: it is an act, almost a cry of the body. The high priest tears his garments after hearing what he deems to be blasphemy (Matthew 26:65, Mark 14:63), and the apostles do the same to manifest their horror and protest (Acts 14:14). The gesture conveys what words would struggle to express.
G1284.origine: The Greek verb combines the preposition "dia" (through, by) with the root "rhegnumi" (to break, to shatter), which reinforces the idea of a rupture or split that goes through. It is a rich verb from late and poetic Greek. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "qara," which means to tear, and which also carries this same emotional weight: it is a physical gesture laden with meaning.
G1284.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Gospels and Acts. Two usages dominate. First, a strictly physical sense: nets break, chains shatter, bonds yield (Luke 5:6; Luke 8:29). Secondly, a ritual and emotional sense: tearing one's garments is a gesture of profound significance in the Jewish context, where it expresses mourning, consternation, or indignation in the face of a serious event. The high priest does this in reaction to the alleged blasphemy of Jesus (Matthew 26:65; Mark 14:63), and Paul and Barnabas do it in reaction to the attempt to sacrifice in their honor (Acts 14:14). In all cases, it is an act that can only be accomplished in a moment of extreme emotional intensity.
G1284.portee: This verb reminds the reader that emotions, even the strongest ones, are expressed in the body and through gestures. It also shows that for the Jews of that time, a simple speech was not enough to manifest horror, indignation, or distress: a gesture was necessary. By seeing the high priest tear his garments, contemporaries immediately understood the gravity of the moment. It is a reminder that in the Bible, faith is never abstract; it is embodied, it is expressed.

sens: To make something understood by presenting it unambiguously
To give a detailed account of what happened
To shed light on the hidden or veiled meaning of something
G1285.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to make clear and distinct what was obscure or confusing. It is to present things in such a way that the listener fully understands. In Matthew 18:31, the servants "report" (explain clearly) to their master everything that has happened: they make known the facts with all the details.

2. The word is also used to report or reveal events, words, or hidden meanings. In Matthew 13:36, the disciples ask Jesus to "explain" the parable of the weeds, meaning to unveil the deeper meaning that they do not grasp themselves.

3. The overall image is that of moving from darkness to light: taking something that was veiled, hidden, or misunderstood, and making it transparent, intelligible, fully clear to the eyes and mind.
G1285.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "dia-" (through) and "sapheō" which comes from the adjective "saphès" meaning "clear, visible, transparent." The basic idea is therefore to pass through, to clarify. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "bâar" (to explain, clarify) and the Aramaic "chawâh" (to make known). The entire root emphasizes the transition from what is obscure to what shines clearly.
G1285.emploi: The verb diasaphéō appears only twice in the New Testament according to the provided usages, both in Matthew. In Matthew 18:31, it describes the concrete action of the servants reporting to their master the events that occurred. In Matthew 13:36, it expresses the disciples' request for Jesus to explain to them, that is, to reveal the hidden meaning of his parables. The context is always one of communication that makes intelligible what was misunderstood or unknown.
G1285.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith also rests on understanding: Jesus does not leave his disciples in doubt; he takes the time to explain to them, to clarify the deep meaning of his teaching. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek the authentic explanation of God's words rather than to remain in confusion, and to believe that God himself helps us understand what he entrusts to us.

sens: To shake or strike violently
To intimidate someone through threat or fear
To obtain money or goods through force, threat, or abuse of power
G1286.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of a violent shake: to shake something or someone forcefully. This is the physical sense of the Greek word, which combines the idea of "over" (dia) with that of "shake" (seiō).

2. Moving into the realm of behavior, it describes intimidation: to frighten someone, to terrorize them through threats to force them to act against their will. This is the figurative use of "to brandish a threat."

3. In its concrete moral sense, it means to extort: to wrench money, goods, or favors from someone through threat, force, or abuse of authority. Luke 3:14 highlights this: John the Baptist forbids soldiers from committing extortion, meaning to abuse their uniform and weapon to steal from civilians.
G1286.origine: The Greek word can be analyzed as a composition: dia (through, by) + seiō (to shake). The basic image is that of a violent shake that goes through something or someone. In Hebrew, the corresponding word in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) is pachad, which means fear or dread. This connection shows that the violent shake quickly becomes a threat and intimidation.
G1286.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:14. John the Baptist uses it to warn the soldiers who come to see him: he forbids them from committing extortion (diaseiō) just like fraud. The context is one of conversion: John asks everyone to live honestly according to their station. For soldiers, this means renouncing the abuse of their military power to steal or threaten civilians. It is a call to concrete moral integrity.
G1286.portee: This word reminds believers that authentic conversion touches the moral heart and daily actions. A converted soldier does not use his authority to terrorize or steal; likewise, no Christian should abuse their power or position to extort anything. It is an exhortation to radical honesty and respect for others.

sens: To scatter, put in disorder (grain, sheep, a crowd)
To drive away, repel (a person, a group)
To waste, squander (a possession, a fortune)
G1287.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to scatter things or beings: when winnowing grain, it is scattered in the air to separate the good from the bad (Matthew 25:24, 26); when the shepherd is struck, the sheep of the flock scatter (Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27).
2. By extension, it means to drive away, chase a crowd, or defeat a group: Mary sings that God "has scattered those who have proud thoughts in their hearts" (Luke 1:51), meaning He has splashed their plans of pride; at the resurrection, the children of God who were scattered will be gathered (John 11:52).
3. Figuratively, it means to waste or squander a fortune: the prodigal son "squandered his property in reckless living" (Luke 15:13), burning through his inheritance in a short time.
G1287.origine: The word is composed of "dia" (through, separation) and "skorpizō" (to scatter); the basic image is that of grain thrown to the wind or sheep fleeing in all directions. The simple verb "skorpizō" also appears in the New Testament, but "diaskorpizō" emphasizes the idea of complete and disorderly scattering. In Hebrew, the Septuagint translates verbs like פּוּץ (poutts, to scatter) and זָרָה (zarah, to winnow, to scatter) with this word.
G1287.emploi: The verb appears about 9 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Synoptics and John. Matthew and Mark use it to describe how the sheep scatter when the shepherd is struck (this is a passage from Zechariah). Luke takes it up in the sense of dissipating a proud crowd or wasting a fortune. John uses it when he recalls that the scattered people must be gathered by the death of Jesus. Acts mentions it for the disciples scattered after Stephen's death. The word thus changes its object and nuance: physical when it concerns sheep or a crowd, moral when it involves waste, spiritual when it concerns the people of God.
G1287.portee: This word makes us feel the disorder, loss, and separation that evil or folly creates. Think of the parable of the prodigal son: to scatter one's possessions is to lose oneself. But it also reminds us that for Jesus and for us, scattering is never final — God gathers those who are scattered, and that is why His death unites the children of God (John 11:52). The word invites us not to waste what we have received and to trust the One who gathers.

sens: To tear or break something by pulling it strongly in opposite directions
To disintegrate, fragment under violence
To be torn to pieces, to be ripped apart
G1288.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of breaking or tearing something by exerting a force that pulls it apart. In Mark 5:4, the demoniac had broken the chains that held him by pulling them with superhuman strength, despite all efforts to control him. It is a violent and complete break, not just a superficial damage.
2. The meaning extends to the idea of disintegration or fragmentation: something that literally breaks into pieces under violence. The verb in the passive expresses this destruction as a process endured.
3. In Acts 23:10, Paul was at risk of being "torn to pieces" by the tumultuous crowd — the verb in the passive expresses the idea of being torn, fragmented, reduced to debris. It is the violence of total destruction.
G1288.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix "dia" (through) and the verb "spaō" (to pull, to tear). The starting image is thus that of pulling something in opposite directions until it breaks. This composition suggests a violent separation, a forced division. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew "nataḳ" which has the same meaning of breaking or tearing away.
G1288.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the passive voice. In Mark 5:4, it describes the superhuman strength of the demoniac who breaks the chains despite attempts to restrain him. In Acts 23:10, it expresses the danger Paul faces of being literally torn to pieces by a hostile crowd in chaos. In both cases, the passive emphasizes a violent and destructive action endured or feared, not a simple ordinary break.
G1288.portee: This word reveals the power of evil and its destructive effects: the demon tearing bonds, human violence threatening to tear apart. But it also shows that this destruction can be stopped — the tribune intervenes to save Paul. The Christian recognizes the urgency of divine protection against forces that seek to destroy us.

sens: To scatter, sow in all directions
To disseminate, cause to spread
To put to flight, disperse a crowd or group
G1289.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of sowing or scattering: seeds are thrown in different directions, as a sower scatters seeds in the field. This is the image carried by the Greek word, composed of "dia" (through, in all directions) and "speirō" (to sow).
2. Figuratively, the word describes the scattering of a group of people: they spread out in various directions, separating. In Acts 8:1, after the murder of Stephen, a great persecution "scattered" all the believers, except the apostles, into the regions of Judea and Samaria.
3. The effect of this scattering is multiplication: those who are "scattered" do not cease to testify, on the contrary. In Acts 8:4, the scattered ones "went about preaching the good news". The word thus suggests a scattering that produces expansion.
G1289.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "speirō" (to sow), from which also comes "spérma" (seed). The prefix "dia" means "through" or "in all directions", giving the idea of sowing everywhere, scattering. In Acts, this word often translates the Hebrew term "pûts" which also means "to scatter" or "to disperse". The biblical image of the sower is thus at the heart of this vocabulary.
G1289.emploi: The verb "scatter" appears only three times in Acts: all concern the persecution that follows Stephen's martyrdom. Each time, the context is the same: believers are forced to leave Jerusalem. However, what the text emphasizes is a paradox: where Satan seeks to crush the Church by scattering it, God accelerates its diffusion. The "scattered" disciples become missionaries against their will. In Acts 11:19, we see these scattered ones spreading as far as Antioch. The word thus expresses not a defeat, but a divine strategy: persecution becomes the seed of multiplication.
G1289.portee: This story of scattering becomes a model for every age: when circumstances distance us from our spiritual anchors, instead of being paralyzed, we are called to continue proclaiming Christ wherever we go. The scattering of Stephen shows that God never loses control: He transforms the plans of His enemies into opportunities for growth. It is a lesson of trust for believers in distress.

sens: The action of dispersing, scattering a group in different places
The fact of being disseminated, spread over a territory or among other peoples
The whole of the dispersed people, a fragmented community
Situation of exile or distance from the country of origin
G1290.detail:
1. The Greek word diaspora primarily refers to the action of sowing or scattering: it comes from dia (through) and speirô (to sow), as if throwing seeds in all directions. It conveys the idea of geographical dispersion, distribution over a vast space (John 7:35 speaks of Jews "dispersed among the Greeks").

2. It then describes the result of this dispersion: the group itself, now fragmented, scattered far from its center. The "foreigners and dispersed in Pontus, Galatia..." (1 Peter 1:1) are believers living in diaspora, far from Jerusalem, the motherland.

3. By extension, diaspora can refer to the state or condition of one living far from their country, as a minority: it is a term that blends the idea of scattering and that of distance. James addresses the "twelve tribes who are in the dispersion" (James 1:1), meaning the Jewish believers scattered throughout the Roman Empire.
G1290.origine: The Greek word diaspora is formed from dia (preposition: through, in all directions) and the root of speirô (to sow). The image is that of the sower throwing seeds in all directions: instead of remaining grouped, they scatter. In ancient Hebrew, the Bible speaks of the Israelites as "scattered" (nidach, za'wa) when the people are exiled or dispersed by God for their unfaithfulness. The Greek diaspora takes up this historical and theological reality.
G1290.emploi: The word appears only three times in the provided New Testament, but it carries a strong theological weight. In John 7:35, the Jews use it to refer to Jewish communities established far from Judea, among the Greeks of the Mediterranean basin: it is a socio-geographical reality. In the two epistles (James 1:1 and 1 Peter 1:1), the term is reused for Christians, especially those of Jewish origin: it loses its purely sociological character to become theological. These epistles address believers who, although geographically dispersed, form one Church. The diaspora is no longer a misfortune or exile, but a missionary opportunity: believers are "sown" throughout the world as witnesses.
G1290.portee: For the modern believer, diaspora reminds us that the Church is not confined to a single place: it is dispersed, alive in all countries and cultures. This transforms our understanding of the Church: we are not isolated, but members of a global community. It is also a call to understand that being a believer can mean living far from our culture or homeland, as "foreigners" — not as lost, but as sown by God to testify. Thus, dispersion becomes a call to faithfulness in a world that is not our own.

sens: To give a clear order or instruction to someone
To impose an explicit directive, with force or insistence
To make an official declaration clearly separating things
G1291.detail:
1. To recommend is to give a clear and direct order. Jesus "commanded" his disciples not to tell anyone that he was the Christ (Matthew 16:20): he was giving them a precise instruction to follow. It is a command, but it can also address several people to unify them around a common course of action.

2. This verb carries the idea of calling for obedience with force or insistence. When Jesus "commanded" the disciples not to speak of the resurrection they had seen (Mark 9:9), he emphasized the order — and ironically, the more he insisted, the more they published it (Mark 7:36). The word highlights the urgency and seriousness of what is being requested.

3. The word can also mean to clearly separate or define things, particularly in a legal or official sense: to give an order that draws a line, establishing what must be done or not done.
G1291.origine: The word comes from the Greek dia- ("through, between") and stello ("to place, arrange"). The basic image is that of drawing a line, separating or distinguishing. In Greek, this verb appears mainly in biblical and later texts. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates several Hebrew words: הִזְהִיר (hizHir, "to warn") in Ezekiel, and בִּדַּל (biddal, "to separate") in Deuteronomy. These Hebrew roots reinforce the idea of a clear separation or distinction.
G1291.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in Mark and Matthew, in contexts where Jesus gives orders to his disciples. In Matthew 16:20 and Mark 5:43, 7:36, 9:9, Jesus "commands" very firmly that certain secrets regarding his identity or miracles not be revealed. In Mark 8:15, he "commands" to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees — it is a warning, a call to vigilance. In Acts 15:24, Christians denounce false apostles who were giving "orders" without mandate. Hebrews 12:20 speaks of "what was commanded" at Mount Sinai. The verb always emphasizes the authority and clarity of the instruction.
G1291.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus taught and commanded with authority — he did not suggest, he ordered. This also reveals the importance of obedience and secrecy in God's plan: certain truths can only be revealed at the right moment. For the Christian, it is an invitation to take Christ's commandments seriously and to convey them with the same clarity and conviction.

sens: Space of time that separates two moments
Duration elapsed between two events
G1292.detail:
1. The word designates the space that elapses between two distinct moments. It is the time that passes between the moment something occurs and the moment something else happens. In Acts 5:7, Peter asks Ananias why Satan has filled his heart, then "about three hours later" (literally "after an interval of three hours"), his wife Sapphira enters — the same interval of time separates them from each other.
2. This word is used to measure or note a distance in time, just as one would measure a physical space. It is a concrete concept: three hours is an interval that can be counted.
G1292.origine: The word comes from the verb διίστημι (diisteimi), which means "to separate", "to place at a distance from each other". The interval is therefore what separates two moments like two objects. The initial image is that of physical space — a distance that separates two things — applied here to the time that separates two events.
G1292.emploi: This word appears clearly only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:7. It is used there to note the delay that separates the moment when Ananias falls dead from the moment when his wife, unaware of what has happened, crosses the threshold. This interval of three hours is narratively significant: it shows that Sapphira, without communication with her husband, will commit the same lie, proving that she was complicit. The word is rare and literary, typical of the more formal style of biblical Greek.
G1292.portee: This word reminds us that time exists — that God creates and governs the moments that pass. In this narrative, the interval of three hours gives the reader time to understand what is really happening: it is not a coincidence, but a revelation that God allows. It also teaches us to pay attention to the details of time: sometimes, what separates two events reveals hidden truth.

sens: Separation or separative between two things
Difference or gap established between people or things
Absence of distinction, uniformity in treatment
G1293.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a separation, a line of demarcation that divides or dissociates two elements. In Exodus 8:23, the Septuagint uses it to mark the separation between the Egyptians and the Israelites during the plagues: God establishes a clear distinction between His people and that of Pharaoh.

2. It then takes on the meaning of "difference" or "distinction" in the sense of unequal treatment: a distinction is recognized between people when they are treated differently according to their status, origin, or function. This is the dominant meaning in Romans 3:22 ("there is no distinction") and Romans 10:12 ("there is no difference"), where Paul asserts that God makes no discrimination between Jews and Greeks in access to salvation through faith.

3. In 1 Corinthians 14:7, the same word denotes a differentiation in sounds: for a flute or a harp to be understood, the notes must have a distinction from one another, they must be clearly distinguishable to make sense.
G1293.origine: The word comes from the verb διαστέλλω (diastello), which literally means "to separate by putting apart": δια- (dia-, "through, in two") + στέλλω (stello, "to place, establish"). The root carries the idea of establishing a line of separation or demarcation. Related words include διαστολή itself and the verb from which it is derived, which evokes the action of setting apart or differentiating. The Hebrew word פְּדוּת (pédhouth) that it translates in Exodus 8:23 evokes a separation or delimitation.
G1293.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. In Romans 3:22 and 10:12, Paul uses it with negation to affirm that justification by faith in Jesus Christ suffers no distinction between Jews and Greeks: all, without difference in religious or ethnic status, are saved by the same faith. This is a crucial point in Pauline theology of equality before God. In 1 Corinthians 14:7, the context is quite different: Paul speaks of music and the importance that the notes of an instrument are clearly distinguished from one another for them to be understood, applying this example to the usefulness of speaking intelligently rather than in incomprehensible tongues.
G1293.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the radical equality of believers before God: there is no favoritism or discrimination in the offer of salvation. The message of Romans 3 and 10 overturns religious prejudices: God does not regard social, ethnic, or religious status, but faith. At the same time, the passage on music reminds us that distinction remains important elsewhere: the gift of speaking intelligibly is making relevant differences to edify the Church.

sens: Twist, distort something
Deny, falsify the meaning or intention of something
Morally corrupt, divert from good
Mislead, induce error
Deviant character, perverse, contrary to righteousness
G1294.detail:
1. The word first evokes the physical image of twisting or deforming: one twists an object to distort it, to disfigure it. In Acts 13:10, the apostle reproaches Elymas for perverting "the straight ways of the Lord" — that is, diverting them, bending them towards evil, as one twists a straight path.
2. In its moral and religious sense, to pervert means to falsify the truth, to distort a message. In Luke 23:2, Jesus is accused of "stirring up" the nation, diverting the people from obedience to Caesar: He is charged with twisting minds towards revolt.
3. The word also describes one who misleads others, who leads them away from the right path. In Acts 20:30, Paul warns that men "will teach perverse things" to divert the disciples — they pervert them by seducing them with false teachings.
4. Used as an adjective ("perverse"), it qualifies a generation or a person whose moral orientation is twisted, crooked in English. Matthew 17:17 and Luke 9:41 speak of a "faithless and perverse generation": it is a people whose spirit has deviated far from God.
G1294.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "dia-" (through, separation) and "strephō" (to turn, twist). The image is one of deep twisting: one does not simply straighten, one twists throughout, distorting to the core. In Hebrew, this word often translates "הָפַךְ" (hâphakh, to overturn, to change), "עָקַשׁ" (âqash, twisted, perverse) and other verbs of inversion or moral deviation.
G1294.emploi: The verb "diastrephō" and its adjective "diestramménos" (perverted) appear seven times in the New Testament. Jesus uses it to describe the "perverse generation" He must face (Matthew and Luke). Paul uses it to denounce false apostles and magicians who divert souls from the faith: Elymas in Cyprus (Acts 13), the false teachers in Asia (Acts 20). The word can be used for a specific action — to pervert someone — or for a quality — to be perverse, to have a twisted mind. It is always a strong term, implying malice and deep deviation.
G1294.portee: This word reminds Christians that the way of God can be distorted, falsified, diverted — not only by error but by malice. It invites vigilance against those who twist the truth to mislead souls. It is also an exhortation to ask God for a right heart and not a perverse one: to keep one's mind turned towards Him, and not diverted by the seductions of the world.

sens: Preserve someone from immediate danger, lead them safely to harbor
Rescue someone from illness, heal them
Aid, protect someone so they escape a threat
G1295.detail:
1. This verb first evokes the concrete idea of leading someone through peril without harm. When the centurion decides to "save" Paul by preventing him from jumping into the water (Acts 27:43), he wants to keep him alive in the face of shipwreck. The word emphasizes the secure passage, the successful crossing: after the shipwreck, the passengers "arrived safely" on shore (Acts 27:44), showing that they reached the destination without incident.
2. The verb also applies to the healing of the sick. When people ask Jesus "only to touch the hem of His garment," they seek to be "healed" (Matthew 14:36) — the word describes how the illness disappears and the person regains their health intact.
3. More broadly, it is to provide aid to someone in need, to pull them from a perilous situation. Whether from a storm, a deserted island, or an infirmity, the word expresses the action of putting someone to safety.
G1295.origine: The Greek word is derived from the preposition διά ("through") and the verb σῴζω ("to save"). This composition reinforces the idea: not only to save, but to save by leading through danger, by traversing the trial. In Hebrew, it often translates מָלַט ("to escape", "to save") and יָשַׁע ("to save", "to deliver"), showing that it is an active protection that leads to a good outcome.
G1295.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, almost always in Luke (Gospel and Acts). In Matthew 14:36, it refers to the healing of the sick who touch Jesus. In the travel narratives of Acts 27-28, during Paul's shipwreck, the word first describes the centurion's intention to preserve Paul (27:43), then the result: all the passengers "arrived safely" (27:44), and the crew "saved themselves" by landing in Malta (28:1). In 1 Peter 3:20, it refers to the salvation of Noah and his family "through the water." Each occurrence emphasizes a successful passage through a concrete threat — illness, storm, peril.
G1295.portee: This word speaks to Christians of divine protection. It reminds us that God does not only want to deliver us from peril but to pull us out "safe and sound" — intact, complete, alive. It is also an image of spiritual healing: to be saved is to pass from the death and disease of sin to new life. Finally, this verb invites trust: like Paul in the shipwreck or the sick near Jesus, we can rely on the One who "saves through."

sens: order emanating from an authority
disposition or arrangement established by an authority
law or official ordinance
G1296.detail:
1. A commandment is an order given by someone who has authority. In Acts 7:53, Stephen reproaches the Israelites for having received the law "according to the commandments of angels" — that is, orders transmitted by divine intermediaries — without respecting it.
2. The word also refers to a disposition, an arrangement established and put in place by the one who commands. In Romans 13:2, the Apostle Paul speaks of "the order that God has established" when referring to civil authorities: it is a divine institution, an organized system that God has set up.
3. By extension, it is a law or an official ordinance, a rule that applies to all those who are subject to this authority.
G1296.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to order, to arrange" (διατάσσω). It is composed of "dia" (through, completely) and the root "tass" which means "to place, to arrange." The initial image is therefore one of putting in order, of complete organization. In Hebrew, the corresponding word often translated is "order" or "decree."
G1296.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Acts 7:53, it refers to the orders transmitted by the angels during the giving of the Law at Sinai — a way of emphasizing the solemnity and importance of the gift of the Law. In Romans 13:2, Paul uses it to speak of the social order that God has established through civil authorities. In both cases, the word reinforces the idea of an organized authority and an order that imposes itself legitimately.
G1296.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's orders and the authorities He establishes are not arbitrary, but thoughtful and just dispositions. In Acts, it emphasizes the greatness of the Law given by God. In Romans, it encourages respect for civil authorities, not just out of fear, but because they are part of the order that God has put in place. It is a call to recognize and honor the order desired by God.

sens: Official command, decree from an authority
Legal disposition or regulation imposed by power
G1297.detail:
1. The word refers to an official command, a decree issued by a sovereign authority — here the Pharaoh of Egypt. It is an order endowed with public authority, which cannot be ignored without risk. In Hebrews 11:23, Moses' parents "were not afraid of the king's order": this order likely prohibited the life of Hebrew male children, yet they hid their son, placing their trust in God above the fear of royal power.
2. More broadly, the word signifies a legal disposition or a regulation imposed by the one who governs — the equivalent of an edict or official decree. It is an act of solemn command, not just an ordinary word.
G1297.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb διατάσσω ("to order, prescribe, arrange"), formed from διά ("through") and τάσσω ("to place, arrange"). The image is one of something that is "put in place" or "arranged" in an official and binding manner. It is an administrative term: it designates the orders that structure the state. In Hebrew, the word נִשְׁתְּוָן (nishtwân) used in Esther 7:11 also carries the meaning of "decree" or "prescription."
G1297.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 11:23. It is an official, administrative term that underscores the authority of the Pharaoh's command. By placing "the king's order" against faith in God, the text shows a contrast: despite the formidable weight of royal authority and the danger of death, Moses' parents chose to trust God. The word also appears in the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament) to translate royal decrees in Esther, confirming its use for official and binding orders.
G1297.portee: This passage encourages the believer to recognize that faith in God is more powerful than the fear of human authorities, however impressive they may be. In the face of the world's "orders" — its pressures, rules, threats — it is possible to prefer obedience to God. It is a call to a primary loyalty to God rather than to earthly powers.

sens: To be deeply agitated, shaken by an emotion or fear
To lose one's inner calm in the face of unexpected news
G1298.detail:
1. The verb expresses a deep and inner agitation: it is to be shaken to the core by what one has just seen or heard. Mary, upon the announcement of the angel, is "troubled" — not just by fear, but by astonishment at something extraordinary and incomprehensible (Luke 1:29).
2. It is to lose emotional and mental balance in the face of the unexpected. The trouble is not superficial: it shakes one's reflection and forces the one who feels it to wonder, to seek to understand what is happening.
G1298.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "dia-" (through, everywhere) added to "tarassō" (to agitate, to trouble). This composition intensifies the simple verb: it is not a mere agitation, but an agitation that permeates the whole person. The prefix "dia-" reinforces the idea that the trouble invades the entire being from within.
G1298.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 1:29, describing Mary's reaction to the greeting of the angel Gabriel. This moment is crucial: the Virgin is not simply surprised, but deeply troubled by a word she does not understand and seeks to grasp its meaning. It is a trouble that leads to meditation, not to panic.
G1298.portee: This word shows that encountering God can shake our certainties and plans. Mary's trouble is not a weakness, but a rightful reaction to the divine mystery: she does not remain passive, she "was pondering" (Luke 1:29). For the believer, this reminds us that God's action can disturb our expectations and calls us to seek to understand His will rather than remain in the tranquility of ignorance.

sens: To give an order, instruction, or directive to someone
To arrange or dispose something according to a plan
To establish, institute a rule or practice
To prescribe what must be obeyed or followed
G1299.detail:
1. The most common meaning is that of an authority giving an order for someone to obey or act: Jesus ordains the servant to rise and eat (Luke 8:55), Claudius ordains the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), the Lord ordains preachers to live by the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is a command that is expected to be executed.
2. The word also refers to the action of arranging, disposing, or putting in order according to an intention: when the governor ordains the centurion to keep Paul with a certain freedom (Acts 24:23), he organizes the conditions of his custody.
3. To ordain can mean to establish or institute something lasting: to appoint elders in the churches (Titus 1:5) or to establish a law, like the Law given by angels according to Galatians 3:19.
4. The word also carries the meaning of what has been prescribed, that which must be obeyed: "all that has been ordained for you" (Luke 17:10) refers to imposed duties, and Jesus spoke of "instructions" to be followed (Matthew 11:1).
G1299.origine: The Greek word διατάσσω (diatassō) comes from διά (dia, "through, in division") and τάσσω (tassō, "to arrange, put in order"). The starting image is that of someone distributing or dividing something by placing each element in its place. The root τάσσω appears in other Greek words of the New Testament related to order and organization. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew שׂוּם (sûm, "to place, establish") and שׁמַר (shamar, "to keep, observe"), which denote the action of laying down a command or enforcing it.
G1299.emploi: The verb appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts, the letters of Paul, and the Gospel of Luke. It expresses concrete orders: Jesus ordains an action (Luke 8:55), political authorities give directives (Acts 18:2, 24:23), the apostles establish rules for the churches (Titus 1:5, 1 Corinthians 16:1). The word is also used to evoke what is established once and for all, like the old Law (Galatians 3:19) or the daily duties of the Christian (Luke 17:10). In passive passages, the emphasis is on the received order and what follows from it: "what has been ordained" refers to the order that must be followed.
G1299.portee: This word reminds us that the believer's life is situated within an order desired by God. The Lord's orders — to live in trust in Him, to serve without glorifying oneself, to obey established authorities — are not suggestions but directives to be fulfilled. Recognizing what has been ordained to us means accepting to be placed in the order that God has decided for us and for His Church.
